utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that we are here in the courtroom. I see that we have the same faces. I would like to greet everybody present, and I see that we have the witness here. Hello, Professor. We are going to continue with this witness today. We are scheduled to start cross-examine. But prior to that, the Prosecutor needs to tell me which documents he will tender into evidence. Please give us the numbers of the documents you want admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The following exhibits I would ask you to admit into evidence: 8559, 0374, 9579, 0996, 7366, 4366, 5312, 775 -- 85, 7097, 9578, 0001, and 8918. This is dossier of Begovina complex. And the exhibits which were given e-court numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see on this list after 5312 it says 775 -- 85. Would you please repeat that number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for this clarification. These documents will be admitted into evidence. On the list of exhibits there are also documents listed for which you did not ask that they be admitted. However, it seems that the Defence plans to use them, and in that case they will become Defence exhibits. I'm looking at Mr. Mundis, who is hiding behind the pillar. I would like to ask him the following in order to facilitate our hearings: Once a document is put to the witness, it would be good if the dossier you are providing to me has the documents in the appropriate order. If you are putting document number 1 to the witness, then make sure that that document is first in my dossier. We would like to avoid the situation in which the registrar has to seek -- look for these documents desperately through the entire material. We would like to avoid such situations. So when the documents are being put to the witness, please make sure that they are in the appropriate order, and these documents need to be in the same order in my dossier. Please go ahead, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Perhaps I misunderstood what -- what Your Honour is asking us to do, but if I understand you correctly, Mr. President, the problem rests in the fact that the dossiers that are provided to the Trial Chamber are done hopefully several days before the witness arrives so that they can be photocopied and prepared and distributed. We often quite -- quite often don't know which -- the order of the documents until we proof the witness, number one; and, of course, number two, in terms of saving time we often make a decision while we're on our feet to skip a document or to re-order the documents in order to save time. And so we will certainly endeavour to give us -- to give Your Honour a good faith best effort in terms of providing the documents in the correct order, but there are certainly problems with that in terms of just the proofing schedule and as well as in-court time schedule that might cause us to jump around in terms of the bundle that gets produced and is provided. So we beg the Court's indulgence as to the document bundle that is provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please try to make sure that you are doing everything you can about this, but please try to understand our position as well. We would like to be sure that this is done in the way that will allow us to work as smoothly as possible. Of course, we are aware of the limitations in that regard. As to the time allotted to the Defence, based on the calculations made by the registry, you have three hours and 44 minutes available to you. That means that this will be the total of time given to the Defence for cross-examination. The Chamber will have one question for the witness, and I will yield the floor to my colleague Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... series of questions. I noted these as we went along, and I think that in the future it will be preferable to put them right away. Mr. Rizvanbegovic, you told us that you were a professor. May I ask what you teach? What subject do you teach?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a professor of the literature of the peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the university in Sarajevo, literature department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You told us yesterday that you were warned by a paper tapped to the door of the house that you would have to leave, but you also said, and this is in the record on the afternoon, page 1, you said that that was pinned on your brother's house. Was it your or your brother's house? And if it was your brother's house, how did you realise that it was addressed to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say that any message was nailed to the house of my brother. I think that there is some kind of a misunderstanding. It was nailed to the -- on the entrance to the main square or main courtyard, and then one can enter into each house from that courtyard. So this order was nailed to the gate leading into this main courtyard from which you can enter other houses. The order had my name on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That -- there must have been a misunderstanding indeed. The next question: You related -- you said your wife tried to pay you a visit and bring you some things to Dretelj. Did she actually succeed or was she sent back without being able to see you or to give you what she had brought for you?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She didn't manage to leave the town. She didn't manage to bring me anything. Nobody was allowed to visit me while I was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said, and for the record, this is page 7, line 6, that young men greeted each other with a certain sign, but I don't recall. Maybe I missed it. Could you be more precise and say what sign it was? I think those were guards at Dretelj. What sign did they make to greet each other? What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were the military policemen driving me, and when they passed other cars, obviously carrying other prisoners, they would greet each other with this Nazi greeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. What -- in Germany it was also called a Hitlergruss, the Hitler greeting. The outstretched right arm with the flat hand. You spoke about ill-treatment that was meted out in the prison to yourself and others. I would like you to clarify who were the people who meted out that ill-treatment. Was it the regular prison guards or was it soldiers that came in from outside and did this for their distraction or for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were both. Unfortunately, both. Very often some other soldiers would come who were not guards, and at least we didn't know them as guards there. They did it for fun. They would fire through the window above our heads while we sat on the floor. They would call out people. They would take them outside of the area where we were, and they would open the door so that we could see how severely they beat them. It was almost daily phenomenon. I knew one of the police commander, Kreso Rajic. He was the secretary of the municipal communist committee before the war. And I asked him to lock the door with another key if possible so that it would prevent such people from entering. Very often they were drunk or under the influence of drugs, and they were the most horrible individuals. But I have to tell you that the guards also engaged in this kind of conduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record, this refers to page 19, line 1. The next point relates to page 25, line 15. You said that in the prison there was a constant fear of, inter alia, being killed. Now, do you know of any cases where prisoners were actually killed there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally did not see a single killing. However, in our shack, the shack where we were, there were people from Prozor and Zepce. They were taken out to dig graves, and upon their return they would say that on that day they buried five people or six people, and so on. So from their stories I knew that some people in the camp had either been killed or died a natural death. I know of one such case where a man suffered a heart attack. So these people were some type of undertakers. That's the kind of work they performed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'm now going to yield the floor to the Defence. I'm not sure who is going to examine the witness. All right. Mr. Karnavas, have you reached an agreement? Who is going to go first? Oh, I see. I apologise. I didn't see you, you were hidden behind the pillar. I really don't know who built this courtroom with two pillars in the middle, but please go ahead. Yes, I can see you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor. My name is Roger Sahota. I would like to ask you some questions on behalf of my client, Mr. Pusic, in relation to events that took place prior to your release in December, 1993. You told us yesterday that you were a leading member of the Bosniak intellectual circle both then and you remain so today; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I feel a bit uncomfortable saying yes, but yes. The answer to your question is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Professor, would you agree, then, that you had a detailed knowledge of the political situation in Bosnia at the time?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that I had a detailed knowledge. I was interested in politics to the same extent as any other intellectual, but not particularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that you, however, knew of and had met many of the significant figures in Bosnian politics at the time?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I didn't have much occasion to meet any individuals from the top echelons of Bosnian political scene. Sarajevo was an encircled town. There was no movement in or out, and I had no occasion to meet people who were in the cabinet or in the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, if that's the people you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: But you would have known the identities of many of the significant figures in the Bosnian government at the time. Would you agree with that, Professor?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I knew them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Can I ask you then, Professor, can you tell the Court whether you had ever heard of or met my client, Mr. Pusic, before your release in 1993?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. It's possible, but we didn't have a contact where we met each other. It is possible that our paths crossed somewhere, but I don't even know who among the accused is Mr. Pusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I'd just like to ask you a few questions about your time in Dretelj and Ljubuski. You were arrested on the 10th of July, 2003; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, on the 1st.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: It's my mistake, Professor. Thank you. But you were detained first at Dretelj and then moved to Ljubuski; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: And you were familiar with the man running the camp at Dretelj, Mr. Sakota; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know him prior to that. I only saw him when he appeared in Dretelj at the time when I as one of the skinniest people and one of the sickest people was designated to go for exchange in Jablanica. That was the first time I saw him. I never met him before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Professor, could you tell us did you ever hear my client's name, Mr. Pusic's name, mentioned during your time in detention at either Ljubuski or at Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name was frequently mentioned. It was said that it was Bero Pusic deciding on exchanges. We didn't know about his role. Once I left the camp, I learned that he was the person in charge of exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I just want to ask you a few questions about your release in December, 1993. Yesterday, you were shown a document which was the certificate for the approval of your release signed by Mr. Pusic. That was identified as Prosecution Exhibit 7097. You told the Court yesterday that you were given that document or handed that document by the warden at Dretelj, Mr. Sakota; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came to the prison in Ljubuski because Dretelj had been shut down several months prior to that, and he brought this release form, and then he took me in his car to Capljina to my family there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: And you were told that you would have to show that document on the border in order to leave the country; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This document and the other document we saw yesterday as one of the exhibits which allowed me to enter the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: If you remember, you told the Court yesterday that although the document was signed by my client, you believe that the authorisation for your release was provided by Perica Jukic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I believe. I see this written on the document, that the authorisation was provided by Perica Jukic. That's what the document says.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Yesterday, during your testimony, you told the Court that you did not know what post Mr. Jukic held, but you thought that he was involved in the military police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was the head of SIS.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Professor, I'd like to show you a document. This was a document that was submitted to the Court by the Prosecution yesterday as Prosecution Exhibit 7016. It hasn't been relied on by the OTP, and I would therefore ask it to be adduced in evidence as a Defence exhibit with the number 6D 0001. And I would also ask for this document to be displayed on the e-court system.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see the content. Oh, yes, I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Could I ask you to read through that document, please, Professor.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is document 0174, Mostar, 2nd of December, 1993. To the Ministry of Defence, to Mr. Perica Jukic, minister personally. "Dear sir, based on the request of the association of writers of Croatia, we ask that you allow free passage of Mr. Fahrudin Rizvanbegovic so that he can leave Mostar and go to a third country. This request is supported by the president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Mate Boban. Sincerely."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Could I ask for the latter half of the document to be displayed on the e-court system, please.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Signed by Vladislav Pogarcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Professor, could you tell us if you've ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't had the occasion to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: The contents are self-explanatory, but I would ask you, do you agree that this appears to be a request for your release approved by Mate Boban himself? Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, clearly it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: And if you look at the bottom left-hand corner, you will see that the letter has also been sent to Ivica Lucic.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Are you aware who Mr. Lucic is?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Could I ask for another document to be produced on the e-court system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, we have to assign a number to this document. Will the registrar do it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... 001. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: This was another document produced by the Prosecution yesterday but not realise on in examination-in-chief. It was it was initially identified as 7026. I would ask for it to be adduced as a Defence exhibit with the number 6D 0002. Professor, could you read through this document, please.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document drawn up two days after that, first a document on the 4th of December, 1993. It says "You should verify on an urgent basis the following: "First of all, was Professor Fahrudin Rizvanbegovic militarily engaged in MOS units. If he has not, you should forward to Tomo Sakota, the warden of the Dretelj prison an approval for him to be released from prison in order to leave abroad. "For the following detainees, the doctor from the medical staff claims that they are mentally retarded and may as such be discharged from prison. Kemal Penava, Enver Penava, Kasim Sator. "This needs to be verified and if this is a true claim they should be approved to be discharged from prison in order to live abroad." Obviously Ivica Lucic is the head of the secretary and information service of the Ministry of Defence, and that is what the stamp says and that is what the signature says.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, Department of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Professor, can you tell us if you've seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I hadn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Having read the contents, is it reasonable to infer that did the security information service approved your release, given what happened afterwards?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the approval which I showed to you as Defence -- which was shown as the first document, it is clear that that was the case. Otherwise, such authority would not have been issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: You note at the bottom of the letter on the left-hand side that there is a list of different bodies that that letter was forwarded to?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now to another document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a number assigned for this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 6D 0002, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Again, this was another document that was submitted to the Court by the Prosecution but not realise on during the course of examination-in-chief and was originally labelled 9577. Could I ask that this be adduced as a Defence exhibit number 6D 0003. And could I ask -- of course I'll ask for the document to be displayed on the e-court system, please. Professor, this is a letter dated the 8th of December, 1993. Could I ask you to read through the contents, please.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the coordinator for human rights, Tomo Sakota. "I didn't know that a coordinator for human rights would be a prison warden. "According to the proposal of Vladislav Pogarcic, the president of the republic of Herceg-Bosna and at the initiative of the associations of writers of Croatia, it is necessary to make it possible for Mr. Fahrudin Rizvanbegovic to freely leave Mostar in order to leave to a third country."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: And could you please read the signature at the bottom of the page, please?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says Perica Jukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: So it would appear this is Perica Jukic writing to warden Sakota; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but at that time he was no longer the warden but the human rights coordinator.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: And you told us yesterday, Professor, that you were escorted from Ljubuski when you were finally released by Mr. Sakota; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Two days after this letter, Mr. Sakota came, and he personally took me to Capljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Can that be identified as document 6D 0003 by the registry, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will the registrar do so.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 0003. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Professor, the documents that will we've just seen show that the sequence of events leading to Mr. Pusic signing the certificate for the approval of your release on the 10th of December began with the letter of the 2nd of December from Mate Boban's chief of staff Mr. Pogarcic. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally, yes. But this is a very simple matter. The name Fahro was only used by the academician Ivo Franges of all my friends. They never wrote the name Fahrudin Rizvanbegovic, here it was always Fahro. It came from Zagreb. It has nothing to do with Mate Boban and Herceg-Bosna. They were just the executors of an order that they received from Zagreb. So that is the essence. Everything else is form. You can call Madam Vesna Franges today because the professor is dead and she can tell you it was only the professor among all these colleagues that called me that name. That is how I actually recognised the hand of Professor Ivo Franges in this, his role in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Would you agree, then, Professor, that the decision to release you was taken long before my client, Mr. Pusic, signed that serve approval on the 10th of December?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was certainly taken before in Zagreb, and it reached your client, but I believe that his role in that matter is wholly insignificant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Would you agree, then, that the evidence suggests that my client was merely signing a certificate rubber stamping a decision taken earlier to release you?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where you're suggesting an answer to me, I cannot say a decided yes because I do not know the background of all this. This is -- these are documents that the Court can appraise in that vein. I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for your fair examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. The following counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Professor, you have been accused in the media of embellishing and in fact lying about some of your experience in the prison. You are aware of that, are you not?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not use such a harsh word which you used so lightly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you in fact, sir, wrote a series of articles or gave interviews accusing some of -- some individuals, in particular Armin Pohara, Sead Pasic, Rusmir Agacevic of having attended the Dretelj camp and then, having been there, throwing cigarettes at the detainees and the detainees throwing the cigarettes back at these individuals who were there to provide humanitarian aid. Do you recall making such statements in the press for which these individuals wrote back accusing you of lying?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably am not entitled to a question, but I should like to ask you this question. Did you read my reply in the same papers on the same date? I replied to those questions, and I believe that I was very correct in contrast to them. They were not correct, and they did not tell the truth. I did tell the truth, and my article was entitled "We can extinguish fire by only -- only by the truth," whereas their article was "Do not add fuel to the fire." But they were untruthful in their claims, wholly, in all their allegations in that article.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Sir --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came there as political people, not as humanitarian workers, and their humanitarian activity was only a cover for their political activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, did you not accuse them of throwing cigarettes at the detainees? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they were throwing cigarettes at prisoners. They carried actually cartons of cigarettes, and they threw them to the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you have the date when -- when this happened? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have a series of articles, but let me continue. And they responded in the press accusing you of lying and distorting the truth about those events, did they not?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you believe them or me? That is up to you. You have my answer. You have their answer. You can, of course, appraise it and weigh it. This is probative material that I have submitted to the Prosecution. I did not lie. It is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are actors. They were the ones doing the lying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, my question wasn't who do I believe. I just want to make sure that you acknowledge that they responded in the press accusing you of lying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You have no reason to ask me any questions about that seeing that you have the document, and the documents are with the Prosecution. You can use them immediately. Just put them on the screen, and I will answer each of your questions immediately, and all of your accusations and allegations immediately. If you do not have them, I have them in my briefcase?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So you have knowledge of them writing back in the press calling you a liar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Karnavas --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This was not exactly the word they used. They used a less harsh term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please. Mr. Karnavas, you are speaking of an article that we do not have, so we feel a bit lost. If you wish the witness to comment on an article, then you have to put it to the witness. It needs to be placed on the screen so that the witness can see that. You're now discussing a matter that we know nothing about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, so there is no question. Mr. President, the problem I'm having is this. I have the articles I'm more than willing but I'm denied effective cross-examination by putting artificial time-lines on me. If I go through all my documents I need four or five hours and I'm only allotted 40 minutes. The gentleman obviously knows what I'm talking about. I'm more than willing to go through this, but then I'm allotted -- give me the time to do effective cross-examination, as my client and all these other clients are entitled to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If you allow a commentary, Mr. Karnavas. Your style may be the usual style in American cross-examination. For us, it is not understandable. What is the purpose of asking the witness a question to which the answer seems to be absolutely obvious? You have the article. You say it's there. He doesn't deny that the article is there, and you seem to pressure him into saying yes on a point which does not bring us forward in the finding of the truth at all. So you must understand that we, not being American Judges, have a certain distance towards your technique and what you regard from your cultural background as matter of fact normal. To us, sometimes it sounds very exotic, and we do not always quite see that this is conducive to the fulfilling of the task which this Court has to fulfil.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, if we go through the transcript, and I would be more than happy to go through the transcript, you will note that he did not answer my question. I posed a question of yes or no. He did not -- I'm entitled to that answer. Now that I've gotten the answer, I'm willing to move on, and it will become obvious why I insisted on that answer, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yesterday, you indicated that there was such a thing called Bosnian language as early as 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, sir, the designation of Bosnian language is older than the name of your country, the United States. It is of 700, 1.000 years old. It has been in existence for some 1.000 years. You obviously are not versed in our history and don't know what you are saying. But I am, and of course I can discuss the subject at some length with you. I was referring to the year 1890. The Bosnian language grammar book from 1890. That was the reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're going to get to that. But yesterday, and I'm quoting from page 22 of yesterday's transcript, I assume it was the first session because the sessions are numbered starting with 1 after each session, you indicated that 37 per cent of the inhabitants registered, and you go on to page 22, and you say "They wanted to have equal status with Croatian and Serbian. What does this mean? It means that all those who would use the Bosniak language regardless of their nationality should be fully equal in this regard to those who call their own language the Croatian language or the Serbian language." You said that, sir, did you not?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say so, of course. All those who wished to speak the Bosnian language can do so, and all those wishing to use that language designation can do so. It was a -- it was one language with three names. Three designations, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, that's a little bit different answer but let's go on. Page 23 at the bottom, you then said --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not a different answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So I take it today you're speaking Croatian, Serbian, and Bosnian at the same time. That's your answer?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And then you went on to say that in 1991, that was when there was the census, that people declared what language they wanted, and that the Bosniak language, I assume you must have meant Bosnian, the Bosniak language was one possibility. Do you recall saying that? It's on page 23. And you go on to say that 37 per cent --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Possibly it was a translation problem. I said Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And as regards this initiative, I launched it when I was the minister, and the Constitutional Court of the Federation actually cancelled the term, the constitutional term Bosniak, and today the only valid term is Bosnian. It's not Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm not here to dispute that. But then you went on to say: "37 per cent of the population declared that the language they used was the Bosnian language." And I assume you meant in the census of 1991. That was the last census that was taken in that country. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Would it surprise you, sir, if I were to tell you that Bosnian as language was not one of the choices one had in declaring the languages on the 1991 census? Would that surprise you?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that that is correct. We have the report of the statistical office showing that 37 per cent actually opted for the name Bosnian language, and you can check it in the statistical almanac, which is a publicly accessible book which you can find at any library of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I have a list of inhabitants, households, habitations and agricultural economy. I have the codex of codes for manual set-up of information. This was the form that was used for the -- for the actual -- for the actual census. If we can pull up on the ELMO, this would be -- we can call it on the e-court, and that would be 1D 00430. Now, I take it you can read Cyrillic. If not, I have it in Latin as well.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cyrillic -- the Cyrillic script is also a script that I use. It is one of my scripts and it is the traditional script of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go on to the next page. Perhaps we can have it enlarged. Now, under 9, I believe it says native language, and then you have possible answers, and it lists the possible choices, does it not? It has Serbo-Croatian, Croatian-Serbian, Serbian, Macedonian, Slovenian, Albanian, Bulgarian, Czech, Greek, Italian, Jewish, Hungarian, German, Polish, Roman, Gypsy, Romanian, Russian, Rusinksi, Slovakian, Turkish, Ukrainian, Vlach, Danish, English, French, Dutch, Norwegian, Swedish, other languages, and unknown?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I have an objection. The Prosecution was not given a copy of this document before the cross-examination. It's quite --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's in the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: It blew from the sky to us now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's in the system. They should have it. They should check their system. They have it. I can give them a hard copy of it, Your Honour, if they're ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Karnavas, the Prosecutor said that when you tender a document which is a document coming from the Defence, before you put it to the witness, before you take the floor, you need to inform the Prosecutor about your intention to use that document. So if you have a hard copy, it would be easier. Once the document is introduced into the e-court, then the Prosecutor cannot access it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I assume it had happened, Your Honour. Obviously it hasn't. We have it over here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you don't see Bosnian there by any chance, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You don't see Bosnian there, do you, as one of the choices?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not, but this is the federal statistical office. I'd like you to use a document of the Bosnian, the statistical office of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is, not those deriving from the Belgrade statistical office. I'm not sure that these are identical statistical figures. I don't think that there are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So are you suggesting that there was --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I personally wrote in the Bosnian -- I personally opted for the Bosnian language. So did my wife and my family, and my wife who gave birth to children that speak the Bosnian language. So it was only normal that they speak that language and that they opted for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So you were saying there were different censuses around the former Yugoslavia. And each republic had their own census, their own rules, their own format, as opposed to the census done at the federal level. Is that what you're suggesting?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not an expert on such things. I don't know what the procedure used was, but I used the data provided by the statistical office of Bosnia and Herzegovina at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, and I take it that you provided that information to the Prosecution to verify that indeed 37 per cent of the population opted for this language called Bosnian, which at least from what I can see wasn't on the list of languages at the time recognised in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslavia, Serbian or Croatian weren't spoken either. Officially the name of the language was Serbo-Croatian or Croato-Serbian, and that was the language was referred to for years officially. I personally took part in the discussion on the declaration and status of Croatian language in 1967, and I know the history behind this name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to have to --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of the effects of the break-up of Yugoslavia, the fact that the languages are now referred to by different names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to have to interrupt you because of time, but I want you to go back to the list and I'm going have to insist for a yes or no, Mr. President and Your Honours, because I see here, first line, Serbo-Croatian. Do you see that, sir? You see that. Can you read it? If not --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that and I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Second line, "Croatian Serbian, Croatian." Right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in the third line "Serbian."

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So it seems at least from my understanding, and I didn't grow up in this system, but we have Serbo-Croatian, Croatian Serbian, and then we have Croatian and Serbian. So at least we have four different languages it would appear. At least you can make a distinction as to which one you wanted; right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you speak English or American?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an identical --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- thing. It is one language with several names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Let's go on then. Now, you say that there was language of Bosnian at the time, and that's what you were insisting on when you were vice-dean at the university; correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I insisted on calling a meeting at the president's office when I asked that the instruction be held in all languages, Croatian, Bosnian, Serbian. That's what I insisted upon. I wanted a multi-linguistic name for one single language. That's not the essence. The essence is that the curriculum also had to be multi-ethnic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let's stick with the language here, okay, because right now you're telling us that in 1991, 1992, there was language recognised in Bosnia-Herzegovina as Bosnian; correct? That's what you want these Judges to believe; correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe in the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I didn't ask you whether you believe in the Judges, sir. And please don't get silly with me.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not as naive as to allow you to get me in -- bogged down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. When was it the first time, sir, when was it the first time, if you are aware, that Bosnian as a language was officially declared in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Do you know that, sir, as a "intellectual"?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, the discussion on the name of the language lasted for several years before the war. After that it was recognised as one of the languages with equal rights. Definitely after the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And it was definitely recognised in the status -- in the census information. Books have been written about this. And if you want, if the Judges want it, I can send you these books with all of the relevant information explained in detail together with the background information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has to do with the equality of the language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not going to pin you on a yes or no because I might get cultural on you. But let's go through the documents. Okay? And I would like to pull on the ELMO, 468. On the e-court, I'm sorry. It's not on the e-court. Okay. If we could put this on the ELMO. We're going to go through a series of documents. This is why, Your Honour, I'm insisting on a yes or no answer on all my questions. It appears that -- excuse me, ma'am, here's the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, on February 24, 1993 -- if you can look at now Article 4. If you could look at Article 4, please. If you could move it up a little bit. If you could look at the second page of the document, and here it is right here. And it says here -- Article 4, please. "In the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbian, Croatian, i.e., Croatian Serbian language, is in use." Do you see that? Latin and Cyrillic. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this is in February of 1993. Then let's go through another document, 469. And the date here is April 8, 1993. Here it says in Article 1: "In the time of war regulation of Article 4 of the constitution of republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina will be suspended of execution." In other words, the Article 4 that we just saw; correct? Do you see that, sir? This is April 8, 1993, suspending Article 4 of the decree of February, 1993. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if I could show you one last document, and this would be 470. And this is dated 29 August, 1993. Here it says, Article 1: "In the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, standard literary language will be," and it goes on, "Bosnian, Serbian, Croatian." It says that -- and the date is 29 August, 1993. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do. I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So you would agree with me at least on this point, that officially the language Bosnian is not in the constitution until August of 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. But I don't know whether you are aware that Croatian wasn't either. Why don't you put back the document showing that the official language is Serbo-Croatian or Croato-Serbian. So not Croatian. Does this mean that the Prosecution will expand their indictment against Mr. Prlic for issuing a decision whereby the instruction at the Mostar university was conducted exclusively in Croatian now that we've established that Croatian was not a constitutional language. Let us not make this more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, what I'm showing --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is quite a complex issue, and you are now entering something that I'm quite an expert in and which is a complex category for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, merely, sir, I was merely trying to point out that yesterday you were less than honest. In fact, you were untruthful yesterday when you said that in 1991 there was a language of Bosnian. In here we see that it wasn't until August of 1993 that the language of Bosnian is put into the constitution. That's the point that I'm trying to drive at.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I regret this. The essence of my answer yesterday was this: I objected to the fact that they wanted the instruction at the Mostar university to be held exclusively in Croatian. That was not constitutional. That language was not a constitutional category, and that's what I objected to. You yourself have just now proven that it wasn't a constitutional category.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, you indicated that you gave a copy of a grammar book dated 1890 to some of your colleagues to give to Dr. Prlic. Do you recall making that statement?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, when you gave a statement to the Prosecution, you never mentioned anything about a grammar book of 1890, let alone giving a grammar book to colleagues to give to Dr. Prlic; correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no reason to do something of the sort. Why do that? That was just a minor episode without relevance. If you wish, I can submit it. It's not a problem at all. It was published by Sima Mesic and Vanja Roric, who are Croats, and it can be reprinted any time you wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, it wasn't the point that this grammar book exists dating back to 1890. The point is that you confabulated yesterday. That's the point I'm trying at. You said something yesterday alluding to the fact that perhaps you gave a document to Dr. Prlic when in fact in your statement you say nothing of the sort. That's the point I'm trying to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand, too. I understand what you're saying. There are thousands of things that I didn't mention in my statement. I've experienced thousands of things and they can't all fit into my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, in your statement, sir, you said that Mr. Prlic wasn't present at the meeting. He wasn't present at any meeting when discussions about the language were going on. That's what you state.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You have to be more specific about that. It's not that I attended the meeting. The meeting was attended by a delegation who informed us about that. I did not attend the meeting. I attended the preparatory work for the meeting. Professor Alija Piric, attorney Damir Sadovic, and the president of the university attended the meeting, the three of them. But I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that you did. But in your statement here you say that Jadranko Prlic was also at the university but he was not present in the meeting. That's what you stated when you gave a -- okay.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I apologise. But that pertains to the meeting of our academic council, not the meeting about the language. Don't try to confuse me. First we spoke about the grammar, and then you switched to another topic. So let it be clear. Professor Prlic did not attend the meeting at the university. He saw the delegation who came to him to ask that three languages be used equally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And would I find that -- the answer that you just gave us, would I find it in your statement because I can't find it. If I gave you your statement, would you be able to locate what you just told us?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which of the two answers, whether he attended the meeting of the academic council at the university or whether he saw the delegation of Bosniaks who came to him asking that all languages be treated equally and that instruction be held in Bosnian language? So which meeting do you have in mind, the one held at the university or the meeting where the delegation came to bring up the issue of the language? These are two completely different matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let me rephrase it again, sir. If I -- if you went through your statement -- if you went through your statement, would you find anywhere that you state that Jadranko Prlic was at a meeting where these discussions were being held? Because I can't find it, and I'll be more than happy to give you a copy and you can search for it. Maybe you can do it during the break to save some time.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the break I will gladly take a look, but I don't see the relevance of it. Professor Prlic definitely met with at that delegation. He saw them. I'm stating it now for the record. And it is certain that the delegation discussed this issue with him, because later on they reported to us about it. I gave you the names of professors in the delegation. I told you who they were. I told you that they informed the council. I don't see why we're dwelling on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, yesterday I just want to go back into one other matter. Yesterday, you talked about forms, report card forms, and you said that they were being printed out in Grude. Do you remember that exchange?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact, you said that they were being printed out in February, 1992, though I notice in your statement you say January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, but it's not a significant fact. It makes no difference whether it was February or January. I think it was in February, but I would need to look at one of the documents. Any documents should have that date. At any rate, it was before the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was declared independent. Before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before Herceg-Bosna was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Perhaps we could put something on the ELMO there for the gentleman to look at. Maybe he can point out to us. And this is a Prosecution Exhibit, 994 -- 92. Now, if you look at the top it says Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, does it not? At the very top.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And this purports to be a -- a report card form, does it not?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we look all the way at the bottom, you'll see there where it does say Grude, and you have 1/ --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A bit more up, please. A bit more. A bit more. We need the very bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Further up, please.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now we can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We can't see it. You need to have the bottom part. This part here, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says 1/92. That is to say January, 1992. I can confirm it now. That's what it says here, January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What if I was to tell you that that 1 does not stand for January?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I know this very well. That means January. For a long time I worked as a principal of a secondary school, and there were some cases where people falsified documents. And when these people were interrogated by police, they -- they interrogated them based on this. This was the key evidence in interrogation. I know this for a fact. This is January, 1992. You can look for experts who can confirm this, but I know for a fact that this means January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And you don't believe that you're wrong.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that I'm right. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used to work there. I know this very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Grude does have a printing company, does it not? Okay.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. When was the republic pronounced, by the way, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1st of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1st of March of 1992. So I guess the folks in Grude must have known already in advance that we were going to have a republic in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so that's why they printed the form in advance. If this was printed in January, 1992, they must have been like fortune-tellers, clairvoyant.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very much so, yes. Very clairvoyant. Even geniuses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. By the way, in January, just to be on the safe side that we understood this point, in January of 1992, what was Bosnia-Herzegovina -- what was it called?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was called the Socialist Republic of Bosnia Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So the folks in Grude in January decided rather than call it socialist republic, simply republic as it was ultimately called later on once it gained its independence?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look at the date of the referendum for independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Check the dates when all of this started. Look at the date when Herceg-Bosna was established, the 19th of November, 1991. And in that context, the document that we saw yesterday, this is how it should be analysed, not in any other context. That was the reason the children didn't want to pick up their report cards or certificates. This is why we raised our voices. That's what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Just one last matter, because I'm running out of time, and I will be lodging something for the record. At that point in time in history, you folks were still being called Muslims as opposed to Bosniak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And when -- when did you actually officially become Bosniaks? When did the name change?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The moment -- actually, you have to know the historical background. It's an archaic word, Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I know. I just want to know officially.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Congress of Bosniak intellectuals held after the Vance-Owen Plan, at the first Congress held a resolution was issued which later on was mandatory for the organs of government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Therefore, at the Congress of Bosniak intellectuals, this was proposed, and later on it became a legal regulation. And while the document is here before us, let me just draw your attention to this report card where it says that the first subject was Croatian language. This is what caused all the problems. This is a report card issued to Muamer Omerika, a Bosniak, a Muslim, and he was issued with this report card where it says Croatian language, and he refused to take this report card, to pick it up. I don't know whether you understand the essence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand the essence and you indicated yearly that there was no difference between the language Croatian, Serbian, and Bosnian. It's the same language. Okay.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's just a matter of equality and human rights to have the language called by their name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I understand that. And incidentally, that report card was issued, since you want to dwell on the point, this was back in 1992, and as we noted, the language didn't officially become Bosnian until August of 1993. So there was no way for them to even call it Bosnian at the time since it didn't exist; correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatian didn't exist, and neither did Bosnian or Serbian. Article 4 of the constitution you showed to us, it says that the language is called Serbo-Croatian or Croato-Serbian. Thus this is not unconstitutional, not that you're speaking about legal law and procedure. This was unconstitutional and this is what we objected to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. You indicated that when you were in Dretelj at one point you saw my client, Mr. Prlic. He was there with the Foreign Minister of Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you say that you think he saw you; right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assumed that, because I tried to sit in the first row so that he could see me. That doesn't mean that he saw me, but he was able to see me, that I did everything I could so that he could notice me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So you're assuming he saw you and recognised you.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I assumed that, which doesn't mean much, because he can say that he hadn't seen me and then we're back at ground zero.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted for him to see me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm sure you did. But the point is, you're making an assumption.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can ask him that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I just want to ask one last. I couldn't help but notice yesterday when you were talking about the situation in Stolac, and you said -- you were talking about how your wife was robbed, and then how -- you said even people with certain skills can launch economic initiatives and then you said something that caught my ear: "And the situation is similar for the poor Croats, similar as far as poor Croats are concerned, because the smuggling people were involved has now ceased." And it seems to me when I read this, I can't help but think that you have a prejudice towards Croats. Could that be the case?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Which is why perhaps you're embellishing all the time?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I was not referring to the times then. I was referring to nowadays because the Prosecutor asked me about the current situation, and I said that people were living differently, Serbs, Croats, and Bosniaks alike. It's hard for everyone. Stolac was the central focal point for smuggling. Not just smuggling of people but drugs and all other things. There were numerous scandals shaking Bosnia-Herzegovina. Please don't twist my words. I was referring to nowadays, to the current period. I was not referring to the past, no. The current moment. And I think I was entirely clear. I apologise if I misspoke and used past tense, but that's not what I meant. I meant the current times. People live very difficultly nowadays. I have no prejudice against Croats. I have more Croatian friends than Bosniaks. Right now there are about 100 households in Zagreb that would take me in. Therefore, do not ascribe me something that I didn't say and that's not true. Some of my best friends in the former Yugoslavia were Croats. This is where I studied, where I did my Ph.D., and these people got my out of prison. What else do you want from me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's why I was curious, because of the comment. Thank you, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for being curious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's 10.30. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, very quickly. I'm aware of the time. On the 8th of May, Your Honour ordered the Defence teams to disclose to the Prosecution any documents that they would be using in cross-examination. I believe the order was one second after we finished. I note for the record that the Prlic team was still releasing documents in the e-court system as late as 10.13 this morning. I also would ask that if any of the remaining teams, Defence teams, that are cross-examining have yet to disclose documents to us, I would appreciate that that be done before we recommence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour. Your Honour. I don't think it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I don't think it is now proper time to discuss that, but it is merely for technical reasons, because this witness was -- on direct he was asked some questions out of the frame of his earlier statements, and all of us, or at least some Defences were working during weekend, and we put those documents in the e-court. We were able to put them during weekend, but the system is not working until this morning or yesterday morning. That is why we were late. And as the documents are coming and we are controlling actually -- for example, my Defence, we are controlling the flow of the documents at this very moment and we release that one document just couple of minutes ago to the Prosecution at the very moment we receive it. So we cannot help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's 10.30. We're going to make a 20-minute break, and then we shall resume the hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume. Mr. Karnavas, as far as the documents are concerned, you may take the floor to request the admission of certain documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President. 1D 00430, 1D 00468, 1D 00469, 1D 00470, and the Prosecution document that we used that was P 9492 should be given a number of 1D 00471.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President those are exhibited under the following references ID 00430, ID 00468, sorry, 1D 00430, 1D 00468, 1D 00469, 1D 00470, and 1D 00471. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And could we have the following Defence team now. We have another hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before I start my cross-examination, I would like to point out that the documents we will be using are not accessible vie e-court for the moment. Unfortunately that's the case. We've provided the Chamber with copies of the documents. Before the commencement of the hearing we also provided the Prosecution with these documents, and when I refer to these documents, I will request that they be shown to the witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Rizvanbegovic.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: My name is Senka Nozica. I will be cross-examining you on behalf of Mr. Stojic. Yesterday, in response to a question from the Prosecution, you mentioned the resolution of the Muslims of Herzegovina. That's Prosecution Exhibit 00374. If possible, could we show the electronic version of this document since we'll be discussing it. Thank you. Yesterday, you said that this is in fact a resolution or a document from the council of Muslim intellectuals. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You also said that this document or the immediate cause for compiling this document was in fact the destruction of the orthodox church, the fact that it was blown up.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the immediate cause.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: As far as blowing up the Orthodox church is concerned -- I can no longer see the document before me. Will this be solved? I have the text, so I'll use the text until the document appears on the screen.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the document before me either.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We have a problem. Just a minute. We have it before us now. Do you see the document?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: With regard to the Orthodox church in Mostar that was blown up, do you know whether prior to this event the church had been set on fire?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it had been set on fire prior to the event, but I do know that it was blown up during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So all you knew was that it had been blown up.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that it had been blown up. I knew that the Zitomislici monastery had been set on fire and blown up before that, and then this church was blown up. These monuments of the first category. We wanted to make sure that other monuments were not destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Since we are speaking in the same language, I would just like to point out that it would be good for both of us to pause between questions and answers for the sake of the court reporters and the interpreters. Do you believe that that reason, that honourable reason for such a reaction was a reason which was in fact the only one which led you to act in this way? The intellectuals in Mostar and Herzegovina, did they have -- or did you have information according to which in October, 1991 the JNA attacked the village of Ravno? Did you know that in May, 1991, the JNA attacked the Unista village? Did you believe that these events were perhaps good reason for your intervention, for the acts you carried out and that protecting the cultural identity of Bosnia-Herzegovina was a good idea, but this resolution was taken a little late for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was the last drop, and when the Orthodox church was blown up, a threshold had been crossed and as a result it was adopt this resolution. So it wasn't the reason for which this resolution was adopted. It was the immediate cause. We'd always been against such things. I'd signed a resolution against the attack on Dubrovnik. I'd participated in prior resolutions that condemned aggression, the destruction of the cultural heritage, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When you say "I," you mean you acted on your personal initiative. It wasn't a fact of other intellectuals. But you as a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina found it necessary to react to certain events?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you must be aware of the fact that the resolution was the initial document issued to gather Muslim intellectuals into an association. This was the initial act on the basis of which this association was formed. Prior to the compiling of this act, we didn't have an association. On the 8th of February [as interpreted], 1992, it was decided to form an association which would enable us to act as an institution.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Apart from what you have just said, what were the reasons for establishing such an association? We have been through quite a bit evidence about this matter, and we are aware of the fact that at the time an aggression had been carried out on Bosnia Herzegovina by the JNA, the Serbian army, call it what you will. So what was the immediate cause for gathering Muslims, intellectuals, in Bosnia and Herzegovina? So they could act or take certain steps, as you say?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you can find the answer in the resolution, but yesterday I said that 42 university professors resigned from the university. They were expelled from the university, practically speaking. They had to organise themselves in order to act. So I would say that this was an honourable resolution.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: While we still have time, I would like to comment on the transcript. Page 40, line 21 it says the 8th of February, 1992, whereas it should say the 8th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see the date in the resolution. It's the 8th of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. In this resolution. Well, could one draw the conclusion that three or four times the resolution refers to the Koran; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And do you know why I'm mentioning this? On the first page you refer to the Koran on two occasions, and on the second page you refer to the Islamic traditions.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you believe that the request under item 1, which concerns the full equality of the Bosnian language, was in a certain sense illegitimate, illegal, because you yourself said today that with regard to the Croatian and Bosnian language and you said that on page 34, line 14, today, you said that the Bosnian and the Croatian language at the time were not languages constitutionally recognised?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, you were in Sarajevo. You were not even aware of the problem in Mostar. You were far away and members of the Presidency who amended the constitution, members of the government et cetera were informed by collaborator such as Hadziosmanovic, they were informed of the good situation in Mostar. In fact, the problem was that people were not informed about matter and they attributed no importance to the matter and I think that this is the reason we have this. And then when you asked me about the Koran and verses, Ajid [phoen] verses from the Koran, we formed an Islamic Community because that was the only organisation we could act through. Other organisations collaborated with Herceg-Bosna or members of the cultural associations had the chequerboard on them all members of the Regional Board of the Party of Democratic Action had the chequerboard on them. They didn't have the golden lily on them. So we were legitimate to the extent that we were the only institution that formed a council.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We'll return to the question of members of the Regional Board of the Party of Democratic Action, but you have just said what I wanted to suggest to you. Referring to the Koran, in fact, implied that it was the Islamic community that had launched the initiative to guard you.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The intellectuals took this initiative, and we wanted to act within this organisation because that was the only institution that made it possible for us to be legitimate, to make it possible for us to be a legitimate organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. This resolution reflects the fact that you wanted to be legitimate. I don't want to enter into a dispute with you with regard to my knowledge or lack of knowledge about the events in that area. Although I was in Sarajevo, I was well-informed of what was going on.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't thinking of you. I was thinking of people in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: My question was about languages. I won't ask you any questions about languages. I know you know much more about it than I do. I won't discuss the matter with you. But could we just confirm what you said today? At the time when this resolution was drafted, Croatian -- the Croatian and Bosnian languages were not constitutionally recognised at the time, as my colleague has already said, Serbo-Croat and Croatian and Serbian were the constitutionally recognised languages; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what it says in the constitution. I can't deny that or confirm it. That's a fact. But that's one's legitimate right. That's in accordance with the law. But here we're talking about the essence of the matter. One language was being imposed on everyone. One curriculum was being imposed. One form, one type of form was being imposed on people. So there was a kind of apartheid against the Bosniaks so we had a he is solution in which we requested equality.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So you used this resolution to request that the Bosnian language be recognised as an equal language in the territory of Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me, what happened after this? Am I right if I say that after the resolution, which was issued in August, there was a meeting of the Muslim organisations of Herzegovina and of independent Muslim intellectuals or, rather, there was a decision on establishing the council of Muslims of Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was an attempt at coordination.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Could we have the following document: 9579, which is a Prosecution document. This is an excerpt from the minutes.
