And in response to a Prosecution question, you discussed this document yesterday. It's an excerpt from the minutes dated the 19th of September, 1992, prosecution document 9579. Before the document appears on the screen, we can move on because you are familiar with this document. Yesterday, on page 28, line 10 of the transcript, you said -- yes, we have the document before us now. You said that this was not an official institution. You said it was a coordinating body.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that that was the case. I wasn't involved in legal matters so I don't know if it was registered anywhere. Cupina, the lawyer, was responsible for such matters so I can't say precisely whether it was registered with the authorities. But in any event, it was a matter of coordinating institutions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. But have you had the opportunity of seeing this agenda and have you had the opportunity of seeing these minutes before, these conclusions? Did you personally receive any decision on the members of the Executive Board? And I'm asking you this question because you, too, were elected as a member of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've seen who the president of the organisation was. I wasn't the president of any of the organisations, and as a result I didn't participate in the preparations for this meeting. I was one of those who was in the hall, and I was proposed as member of the Executive Board at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But on the first page you would agree with me if I said that you, all of you who were there, adopted a decision on establishing the council of Muslims of Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because it has to do with your assessment that it wasn't an official institution with your assessment that it was a coordinating body. If we have a look at the second page could we have the second page in Croatian, Bosnian, and Serbian language. Article 7 says: "The council convenes sessions. Between sessions the executive committee shall act as the council." Article 8 says: "The council is of a temporary character and works at the time of war and imminent threat of war and up until the time civilian democratic authority is established in accordance with the constitutional and legal system in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Then we have Article 9 and the bodies that have been elected. With regard to Article 7, let's have a look at Article 7. As a member of the Executive Board you can see that it says that the council convenes sessions and that the Executive Board acts as the council when sessions are not held. So could we conclude that it was an informal body or does this body nevertheless have all the legal elements that are required when taking decisions regardless of whether this body was registered or not. I won't ask you whether it was registered or not you yourself said that it wasn't registered but does this decision show that we're talking about a formal body with precise tasks and a specific role in society?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could ask you that question. I'm not a lawyer so I can't answer such a delicate such a sensitive legal question. I'm an intellectual and I can interpret a text. I know the reasons for which we established this body and I do know that it was necessary to establish the conclusions we see before us. So I couldn't really provide you with an answer to that specific question. The lawyer Cupina and others were involved in this I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether you adopted certain conclusions? You said "we were a coordinating body." Did you adopt certain conclusions on that day?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The working, the acting Presidency proposed certain conclusions which were then adopted.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. If we have a look at those conclusions which were adopted and we can see them on page 3 of these minutes. In Article 1 it says a we condemn the acts of the Regional Board of the SDA in Herzegovina and especially the acts of the president Dr. Ismet Hadzihasanovic with regard to defending the rights of the Muslims of Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Have a look at item 2. We're taking away the right of further representation of the Muslims of Herzegovina. We're taking the right away from the president of the regional committee of the SDA of Herzegovina Dr. Ismet Hadziosmanovic and the lawyer Camil Salahovic from Mostar. Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: My question is what did you think when these were being adopted?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean me personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you think that such a decision amounted to a decision of practically replacing the members of the regional SDA board by depriving them of the right to further represent the interests of the citizens?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. This is a conclusion generally divesting the right of further representation to just them, because until that time they were the only ones vested with such representation, and this was actually one of the major reasons why the meeting was convened, so that a coordination board could discuss these problems and suggest solutions. Namely, we were not authorised. We did not have the right to impose such conclusions on political party, and the council consisted of different representatives of different political parties and cultural organisations. You saw the list yourself. We just wanted all institutions to be involved in decision-making; namely, all those Muslims who were faced with different problems at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. But that's not an answer to my question. By this conclusion, you divest these two people of the right of representation.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you think that we had the power to divest them of that capacity? It was only by moral strength that we wanted to actually bring inference to bear that they act in a different way, that our partners with whom we wanted to talk, namely the authorities, the cultural institutions, the religious institutions, we wanted to be able in all such cases not to be represented by that party and its president, Mr. Hadziosmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please, you say we are suggesting. But you're not suggesting. What is written here is the right is generally deprived of further representation and so on.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm asking about what you exactly said in your answer. This is a political party that is politically registered, that it has its bodies and the way these bodies are elected. Can anyone, if they so wish, through legal procedure divest anyone of the right of further representation if that someone was legally set up in legal procedure?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, the SDA party has a small following, and those people actually usurped the right, the political party usurped the right as the sole party and sole group of people to keep representing the Bosniaks as a whole throughout this period. We wanted to divest of them that particular right. We cannot have Ismet Hadziosmanovic discussing for instance religious matters with the bishop or cultural matters being discussed with cultural representatives. We wanted to divest them of that right. Now, whether they actually discontinued that practice, they didn't. They continued to act in this way. But at all our meetings we sought to stop that practice, to put an end. We did not interfere in the internal matters of the party.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did attorney Camil Salihovic and Mr. Ismet Hadziosmanovic continue to be members of the Regional Board after these events?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. This was their legitimate right because unless ousted by their own party bodies, they still held their functions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Were they replaced in a legitimate way?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were replaced in a legitimate way by the boards of the individual municipalities following an initiative for the convening of a meeting of the Regional Board when Mr. Hadziosmanovic was replaced by a member of the Presidency of that party, Mr. Demirovic. And Hadziosmanovic was the city councillor, president of the city council of Mostar so he was just actually transferred to another post but it's an internal party matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Precisely because we are dealing with internal party matters, that is why I indicated that this conclusion in a certain way actually encroaches about party matters, SDA party matters.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree. This is not encroachment upon party matters. These are matters that concern the entire people.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did anyone actually forbid the party members in Mostar to deal with anyone else in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they did. They just wanted to deal with Hadziosmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And what was the actual case in religious matters?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can talk to the mufti about specific matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When -- when on the 19th of September, 1992, the board was set up, do you remember that a press conference was held?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that there was a press conference, but I didn't take part in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Were you informed that a memorandum had been drawn up on that occasion on the situation and problems in Mostar and Herzegovina which was drawn up by the cultural circle of Mostar Muslims as part of the Islamic Community?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. Perhaps it was so. Could have been the case, but I didn't participates in any such actions and you have to bear in mind that I lived in Stolac myself so I would have to go and attend these meetings and many of the meetings I actually did not attend. So I was not involved in that particular activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But I will show you this memorandum anyhow, and can I have it put on the screen. The number is 290007. The reason being that it is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Actually, interpreter's correction, 2D 0007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: We have this document, but it is not translated. I don't know how many pages does my learned colleague want to use during her cross-examination. It's quite a large document. It is not translated. Maybe at least we should -- we have the right to have translated relevant pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I should like to address the Prosecution now. It would be customary for such documents to be -- to be translated in advance. If we tender it now it will only receive an identification mark. And please show the document to the witness. In that case, ask him to read the relevant sections and then we shall heard -- hear the -- an oral translation of the -- of the document. And please read slowly.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I should like to inform you that the Defence team of Mr. Praljak gave this document for translation on the 21st of December, 2005. The number being 5D 352-19, and the entire document will be submitted in due time. But it is a voluminous piece of paper, so we were unable to prepare the translation on time. For today I will just present the witness the first page just to see if he actually did participate in the compiling of this memorandum. So if you can please have the document placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you see the first page of this memo? Please take a look at it. Actually, the second page, which gives the table of contents and actually says that it was made by the cultural circle of Muslims in Mostar. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but this is not the same circle. I myself am not aware of this document. I have no knowledge of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm confused a bit now. Are you saying that there existed two circles?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know about this circle that you are referring to, and this is not an official paper. This was something which was on their agenda probably, but I myself have never seen it before. I did not participate in such a meeting and I really have no information whatsoever about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, then, in that case we shall not go through the document any longer if the witness says that he is not aware of it at all. But I should like to inform you, you think you should know it, that the council of the Muslims of Herzegovina together with representatives of the cultural circle of Muslims of Mostar at a press conference --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see that you're referring to two institutions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, yes, but this resolution was made by this first institution.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It was drawn up by the Muslim intellectuals. Tell me, when the Muslim -- the council of Muslim intellectuals of Herzegovina was set up, was one of this constituent meeting also the cultural circle of Mostar intellectuals?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, it wasn't. They were not. You can see the signature on the paper, and as far as I remember, I was in the audience. I did not take part in the preparations. You can see that the only institutions are listed in the first minutes of meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Then let us go back to the Prosecution document number 9579, an excerpt from the minutes, page 1. Could you please zoom it in. This first part which immediately after -- under the title, whom did Mr. Faruk Cupina represent at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that he was a representative of the cultural circle of Muslims of Herzegovina as the technical organiser.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Was he a member of the cultural circle of Muslims of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. I didn't take any part in any of this, so I really don't know. I took no part in any preparations for this event. I only attended the large Assembly of 300 or so intellectuals, and I was elected to the Executive Board at that meeting, at that Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But tell me, did you attend the press conference then?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not that I remember. I don't see why I should have been there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Then please can I have the document shown, Defence Exhibit 2D 0017. They've just informed me that we have it in e-court, so we can try and see it in that way. Are you familiar with this decision? It -- it is a decision of the Crisis Staff of the municipality of 29th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar with it. I had no contact with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please can you enlarge this part which lists the members, the names and surnames of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this refers to Mostar. I belonged to Stolac, not to the Municipal Assembly of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm showing you this because you participated in the Assembly which adopted a decision on the setting up of a council of Muslims of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the conclusion was adopted as we just read to divest the -- of the right of the further representations of Muslims in Herzegovina, Mr. Ismet Hadziosmanovic. So that is the part I would like us to be able to see, please. If you can, yes, just go down a bit, the members of the Crisis Staff. So when this decision was taken on setting up the council of Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as you did discuss at the session, as you said to the Prosecutor yesterday, the situation in Mostar, everything that was going on at that time, and you did adopt a number of conclusions on the basis of the situation discussed. So I'm now asking you, did you know of the existence of the Crisis Staff in Mostar, and did you know at the moment when you were taking that decision to establish the council of Muslims of Herzegovina who the members of the Crisis Staff were in?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know. I knew from the media that this Dusan was replaced with the advent of the HVO and that the legitimately elected mayor of Mostar was Mr. Gagro. And I don't know anything specific because I was not in Mostar at that time, and I was not associated with it in any way.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please look at these names. You talked about Mr. Gagro.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the president of Mostar, so I knew about him from the media as well. Not personally. I think these are the people, different party representatives.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Zijad Demirovic, party member?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the SDA, in the Presidency he was one of the members.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And Ismet Hadziosmanovic?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was also in the Presidency, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'll be careful henceforth. Mr. Hadziosmanovic so remained, as you said, in this post. Who actually became president of the Regional Board of the SDA for Mostar at that time?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was an internal matter of the party. I know as a citizen and as an intellectual that Zijad Demirovic was the Regional Board president, and Ismet Hadziosmanovic for Mostar. Otherwise, I was not associated with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The conclusions in the decisions on the founding of a council of Muslims of Herzegovina, you did not refer to Mr. Demirovic.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not an official. He was just a member of the Presidency of that party. We just wanted the party -- the president of one party. We were against having such a person or one party only being the party that would represent a whole people.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And was Camil Salihovic a member of the party?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No he was just a gofer in the party. And he often would actually represent that he was doing this on behalf of Hadziosmanovic that he had such authority. But I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So, Mr. Professor --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was certainly so. I was only in the auditorium. These conclusions were just presented to the members of the council and the 300 of us adopted them by acclamation. We said that they were good. We did not dwell on the details.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Professor, yesterday I got the impression that you were behind or you supported all of these conclusions when giving your statement, but it seems that I wasn't right in concluding that. Will you agree with me that you didn't ask for Muslims of Bosnia and Herzegovina not to be represented only by presidents of certain parties, including Mr. Hadziosmanovic, you also objected to membership, but you didn't ask that Zijad Demirovic stop representing Muslims.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was no reason for that because he never had such authorities as did Hadziosmanovic, because this is how he presented matters. He gave the impression that he was authorised. The essence is that these two people took it as their right, one as president and the other one acting on the orders of the president to represent the entire nation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please not overlap. It is impossible to interpret if they continue to overlap. And could the counsel please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What is your opinion? What was this about? Was it that they gave the authorisation to the HVO to take over the defence or, rather, the Municipal Staff in Mostar was to take over the defence of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Most likely it was that, but I can't speak too much about this because I was not involved in it. These decisions were taken in Mostar. I was in Mostar only occasionally because I was in Stolac throughout that time. And I took part in this as an educated person, not as a political individual.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. We have the document. Let us now read Article II, signed by these members including those who you believed were inappropriate to continue to represent you but who continued to represent the Muslim people through the SDA. Item II says, "The defence and the protection of the city of Mostar mentioned in Article I is hereby entrusted to the Croatian Defence Council, Municipal Staff in Mostar, and members of the Ministry of the Interior centre in Mostar." So the gentlemen listed here and others adopted this decision and signed it. I'm asking you, even though I know that you were not present, you didn't take part in this, but I'm asking you with a view to certain decisions that you later adopted within the circle of Muslims intellectuals.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never took part in the part of Muslim intellectuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You were participant in the council of Muslim intellectuals?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But could I please see the date of this decision?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could speakers please not overlap. It is impossible to interpret.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The date is April 29, 1992?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 29th April, 1992. I was unable to leave Stolac because it was occupied by Chetniks. I was unable to go to Stolac until June of 1992. Therefore I don't see why you are asking me this. There was no way I could participate in this.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, but this decision was adopted before the council of intellectuals of Bosnia and Herzegovina was established and in that session you discussed the issue of who represented you up until that time and in what way. And it was your conclusion at the time that certain individuals collaborated with the HVO. You didn't have to know about this decision when you were discussing this, but if you were deciding on who was going to represent henceforth the Muslims, then I think it would have been logical for you to know who passed what decisions in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I assume that hundreds of decisions were adopted that I knew nothing about because they were different organs. What you're trying to do is lead me into a different sort of situation. We established the coordinating board composed of -- with representatives of all legitimate bodies in which Muslims participated. So what we wanted was for all these legitimate organisations who delegated representatives, for them to represent Muslims who would have the support of citizens. We wanted for that institution to take part in discussions, adoption of decisions and so on. We wanted to take part if public life, otherwise, everybody was ostracised from the public life. And it was only one party, a local oligarchy who took it upon themselves the right to represent the entire nation, ignoring all of the other political parties, all other organs ignoring all political public and religious establishment of the people. I apologise. I apologise to the interpreters. My daughter is an interpreter here, and she's telling me that we're awful.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Professor, I said nothing different. All I said was that if the decision is being taken that somebody is no longer entitled to represent the Muslims of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it would have been logical for me to assume that you should have known who until then adopted crucial decisions on representations of -- on representation of Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in Mostar. I consider this to be a crucial decision?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You may continue to assume so.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I have just one more question for you. Could we now see on e-court document 2D 00020. Have you ever had occasion to see these conclusions adopted by the SDA in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This wasn't in Sarajevo. It was in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. That's the party from Sarajevo, but the session was held in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here, but I never saw this decision before this.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In that case, with your permission, I will read out some portions of it. Even though you never saw this document before, I believe it to be an exceptionally important document. And in item 5 it says precisely what we have on the screen now. "The establishment of Muslim national councils in certain areas in Bosnia and Herzegovina is not an appropriate response to certain pressure and unilateral steps taken by the HVO, the difficulties and functioning of the state authorities and insufficient activity of the SDA." If we can see the top of this document, please, we can see that it was adopt -- or, rather, the session was held on the 3rd, 4th, and 5th ever October. And then at the bottom we can see that this document or, rather, the conclusions were made public on the 5th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour. I want an objection. The witness clearly claimed that he had never seen this document, and he is being now cross-examined about this document. It's relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What is the relevance? The question that was put to the witness, how relevant was it since the witness never saw this document before? You drew our attention to item 5 of this document. What is your question to the witness that would be useful and important for us, the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will put a question to the witness and you will see that it is relevant for what I want to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead. Please put your question and then we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know who at that time was the acting president of the Party of Democratic Action, the SDA?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about it. I know nothing about that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you think it was possible that it was Mr. Mirsad Ceman?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the entire period or just in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll just ask to have the following documents admitted into evidence, please. Defence Exhibit 2D 0007, 2D 00017, and -- I apologise. These are two Prosecution exhibits that I just referred to. 00374 is Defence Exhibit 2D 0019. And then we have another Defence exhibit. This is Prosecution Exhibit 2579.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction 9579.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which has now been given number 2D 00023. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Those two documents will be admitted under the following references: 2D 00019 and 2D 00023. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I believe that it is. If I have anything to complain about, I'll let you know towards the ends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. After the break -- we have another 45 minutes before the break, and we may start now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would rather not disturb our customary schedule. I can continue now and then we can interrupt for the break. But before I begin with my cross-examination, I would like to ask the Trial Chamber to allot about five minutes to my client. He has a topic that he would like to examine on, the topic that was mentioned in direct examination and in cross-examination, and it just so happens my client is quite knowledgeable about this issue. It involves the language. So if you could pleased give him five minutes for that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Professor, I never have enough time so therefore I would like you to give me very simple answers to my very simple questions.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This issue is not a simple one, but we will attempt. We will do our best.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: The Muslims in a formal, legal sense became a nation in 1974 in the constitution. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not become a nation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: No. I meant in the formal legal sense?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to that, in the 1963 constitution, there was that category as well, but they were not called Muslims. They were called something else then.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please, my question was quite specific. The Muslims became a formal legal category in 1974.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under that name, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. At that time, they were not given a right to their language to which they are entitled. Don't think that I think that they're not entitled to it. But at the time, they were not given that right.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We asked to be called Bosniaks at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did not get that right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And that lasted until 1993. And it was only in 1993 that in the formal legal sense that language was known as Bosnian language.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bosnia-Herzegovina, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You were a member of the League of Communists?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you ever through various declarations ask that this undeniable right of the people be given to them?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to communists?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, to communists.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you were a communist yourself, so you should know about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I apologise, but I wasn't. Your information is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information. I was not interested in you at all until you took part in these events.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You are a witness, not a judge here.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you about a political party and its --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a complete outsider in the League of Communists. I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You are taking away from my time. I'm not facing you as a judge. You're a witness here. So I ask you that, as a witness, you give very specific answers to my very specific questions.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: For 17 years the Muslims existed as a nation in the formal legal sense, but in Tito's Yugoslavia, in the formal legal sense they were not given the right to refer to the language under their own name; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In the constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia there is a list of languages which the individuals and peoples in the SFRY were entitled to use. We saw that in the document shown by Michael Karnavas. It has a very specific enumeration listing Serbo-Croatian, Croato-Serbian, Serbian, and Croatian, which means that in the entire territory of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the Croatian language was a constitutional category, and it could be used as a native language of Croats without incurring any legal punishment. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't need an explanation.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why don't you let me explain? You can't hold a speech without letting me explain.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. You gave us your answer. That's enough. The documents will show who is right and who isn't. We are not here to listen to various explanations. Now, you are an expert on literature.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you ever write about linguistic problems?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you write grammars?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you write about orthography?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you ever right a dictionary?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you ever write something about syntax?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: My time is running out, but I'd like to show something else here. You were -- you wrote about Croatian literature.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Including Croatian literature.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Would you agree that Marin Drzic is one of the most important drama writers in Croatian literature?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you hear of Reljkovic Matija as a writer?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I studied in Zagreb. Naturally I heard this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Professor, just give me a yes or no. Did you hear of him?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please don't act that way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You are taking away from my time. Did you hear of him?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You took away half of my life, man. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of Hektorovic?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally I did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: With the Trial Chamber's leave, and the interpreter's help, please try and translate the following verses written by Marin Drzic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot interpret this verse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, please recite this but slowly, because you were so fast that the interpreters couldn't do it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no one understands this. I'll repeat this slowly. Ask the Croats who are sitting here and Mr. Rizvanbegovic whether he understood anything. The interpreters cannot interpret this. This -- they do not know the language of the Croatian aristocrats.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The gentleman is confusing speech and standard language. As a French mirrors an Italian, do you understand language from the 15th or 16th century.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You're giving a lecture. That is court.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not asking you anything. I'm asking the Judges.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the professor is not giving a lecture here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are giving a lecture now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, put your question to the witness and we'll see what the professor replies.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Professor, this text of Marin Drzic, one of the greatest writers of Croatia and with reference to his best known work, the Dundo Maroje, well, did you understand anything I recited from this text?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally I understood something. If I had the text in front of me, I would be able to translate all of it. There'd be no difference between your translation or the translation of your colleagues here. If I had the text in fronts of me, I would be able to understand the text. How else could I read Dundo Maroje, but you must be aware of the fact that a play can have speech or a local dialect in it, and that is the case in the verse that you recited. So I don't know why you're asking this question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: When you say that Marin Drzic has -- contains a language which is the local dialect from Dubrovnik --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. That's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: How can the best playwright use a local speech?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miroslav Krleza, the best-known Croatian writer, wrote something in the Kajkafski dialect, in the local speech.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Unfortunately this kind of a discussion leads nowhere. I believe that the Trial Chamber should keep to facts. And as to interpretation of fact of those who in Mostar acted after Vukovar, after Zadar, after Mostar, as to those who questioned the legal status of the Croatian -- well, such people are not intellectuals, Professor, but I believe that the Trial Chamber will keep to the facts. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was an attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, you have half an hour before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And to finish this subject matter about the language, I would like to show to the witness one document. It is in the electronic court. It is number 3D 00182.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, before we see this document on the screen, you mentioned Zijad Demirovic on a number of occasions, the SDA party president. We now have the document before us. This is a letter he drafted on the 8th of March, 1993. He wrote to the Minister for Science and Education -- to the Ministry for Science and Education in the republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the first paragraph, in March 1993, Mr. Demirovic mentioned certain events in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he said that, "We suggest that you start the procedure for the modification of the constitutional and legal status of the language in our multinational and multi-cultural community. Regarding the fact that the constitutional legal category has been exhausted with regard to the Serbian, Croatian, and Croatian Serbian language as official languages of all nations that live in Bosnia-Herzegovina, our initiative is an urgent one and we believe that it is necessary to act immediately, without any delay." So there's a request to legalise the issue of the existence of the Bosnian language. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw in the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina the date when this occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Please. We have very little time. Everyone has been allocated a certain amount of time for you. So please answer my questions by saying yes or no. That's how I'll put my questions to you. If there's anything you'd like to add, the Prosecution who called you are here, and you can give us a sign and they can ask you additional questions. All I'm asking you, is you've seen this letter? You've read through this paragraph. The -- would you agree that this is an initiative launched by the SDA in order to solve the issue of introducing the Bosnian language as a legally recognised language? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I agree with that. It's a matter for the party who acted on this initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So it's quite clear that until this issue was dealt with and later there was an amendment to the constitution, my colleague asked you about this, but we have seen that the Bosnian language as a legally recognised and constitutionally recognised language in 1992 and right up until the summer of 1993 did not in fact exist. It did not exist in legal terms.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Bosnian Croatian or Serbian did not exist in those terms. Only Serbo-Croat and Croato-Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... break for 12.00 or -- or should we go until quarter past twelve?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We could have the break now or we could have the break at half past twelve or at quarter past twelve, as you wish. It's for you to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all the same to me, but I couldn't really remember whether the break was at 12.00 or 12.15, but I believe we usually had the break at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Usually we would have the break at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will then continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rizvanbegovic, in your testimony yesterday, page 10, line 16 of the transcript, you mentioned Alija Rizvanbegovic, who was the president of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Of the Executive Board of Stolac municipality. Until the Croats fled. I think that's what you said.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, until the Croats returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Would you agree that when the JNA forces arrived and the so-called Territorial Defence forces or, rather, Serbs from other areas, when the aggression was launched on Stolac, the Croats on the whole fled from Stolac?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And from the surrounding villages?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Many Muslim inhabitants also fled.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A fairly small number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But some did?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have the opportunity of observing that, but on the basis of the people I saw in the town, I didn't -- realised that most of them hadn't fled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: With regard to the Muslim inhabitants from the Dobravaska Visoravan village, did they flee?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know most of them didn't. Some of them fled. They saw that other were fleeing, but most of them did not flee.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that those who did flee fled before the Serbian aggression?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And they fled because they were afraid?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And many of them crossed the Neretva River to reach Mostar and other villages on the other bank of the Neretva?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to Mostar. Mostar is to the north. But to Capljina, in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. But they went in the direction of Capljina?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that was the case because there was no reason to go to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Are you aware of the fact that most of them crossed Neretva near Pocitelj where there was an improvised ferry and boats?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware at the time but that's what my friends told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: One could say that this had been "organised." The cross had been organised.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything had been organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The people were met on the other side and that was controlled by Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were no forces there at the time. There was still a lot of chaos then, but I don't know whether they were met there. I wasn't on that side so I couldn't observe anything there. I was at Stolac. I know nothing about that. All I know is what I heard from others. People told me about their experiences but that's not something I could testify about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I understand that, but given all the social activities that you have spoken about at length, you were obviously a person who was very well-informed. And you tried to obtain information about the events?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, please slow down a little because it's difficult to follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Natural little we know that you weren't there given your testimony, but if you were informed of the events at the time in Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you hear anything about people crossing the river and about this being organised?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I can't deny that. That's what I heard from other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about the HVO meeting them there in an organised manner?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everyone mentioned boats that took them over the river but I don't know whether the HVO was there. People speak about the Croats meeting them or the people from Capljina, but they didn't mention the HVO. They spoke in these ethnic categories. But, yes, they were met by people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said that not a single shot was fired in Stolac, but it is true to say that people were arrested in Stolac while Stolac was under the JNA control?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was mostly the Serbs who were arrested. Stolac was a multi-ethnic town, an old town, and people were on relatively good terms with each other. The Serbs arrested those who didn't want to join the Serbian army because they thought it was a Chetnik army or they recognised Chetniks in that army. Many people even fled from their positions. There were two men who hid in my house. One was the former president of the municipality at the time of the communist system, Risto Ruzic. He's now in Stolac and he's still me friend and he spent over two months in my house. The second person a second man who fled from the line arrived in my house with a rifle. I took his rifle to his wife and he also spent two months in my house. So I risked my life so that those people who didn't want to participate in the aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina could be protected. I protected them. They were my friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. But I'm saying that Croats were also arrested, about 180 Croats from Stolac and the villages in the vicinity were actually taken away to Bileca and on the whole they were exchanged and returned alive later on.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that from people -- about people in another city, in Dubrava, but I know nothing about Stolac. I know that both southern Croats were arrested in Dubrava and they were taken to a camp because when they were released from the camp I was one of those who met them, provided them with food, and other forms of care.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. I haven't had the opportunity of checking the transcript or the revised transcript, but at one point in the transcript it seems that you said that in June the HVO liberated that area that includes Stolac and Dubrovnik plateau. They liberated it from the JNA who withdrew. I think you also mentioned HSP forces.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean the HSP forces, the HOS?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, the HOS.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they entered Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And there were the HVO forces too?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they came after them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So they liberated Stolac.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You forgot the Dubrava plateau, the Dubrava battalion. That was the third force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let's take this step-by-step. At that time, the Muslim forces or those who preceded the Bregava Brigade were under a Joint Command. They fought together with the HVO. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What's the problem?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you also mentioned that certain forces had put out the Croatian coat of arms at various places in town. I'd just like to be clear about something. Are you talking about the coat of arms of the Croats or are you talking about the official coat of arms of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there were certain institutions such as the municipality and the post office where they had placed signs with the coat of arms of the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The coat of arms of the Croats and not an official state coat of arms that belonged to the State of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the case that they didn't use the official coat of arms of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You said that you came to Mostar about the 25th of June, after liberation of Stolac. Mostar had been significantly destroyed. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that all the bridges had been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether all of them had been destroyed. When I arrived there, I came from Medjugorje because it wasn't possible to get there via Buna, so I couldn't see which bridges were destroyed and which weren't. I crossed the old bridge which hadn't been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That's correct. The old bridge hadn't been destroyed. Had it didn't damaged at the time?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only to a slight extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour. Your Honour. I would like some clarification. The witness and the counsel are talking about the 25th of June of which year?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was referring to 1992. I did so at the beginning of my question. I was referring to the liberation of Stolac yesterday and I also referred to the page of the transcript where the witness talked about this. It was the liberation of Stolac in June 1992, and then the witness said that on the 25th of June, 1992, he went to Mostar for the first time. So we know which date was concerned.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't go to the bridge on that day. It was a few days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Professor, let's simplify matters and try to answer my questions frankly. Did you have negative impressions given the extent of the destruction in Mostar since after several months you returned to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the part around the old bridge, the shops there, et cetera, had been significantly damaged. I know that there were certain liberation forces that had damaged and set that part of town on fire. That's what I was told, but I don't know whether that was true or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. Professor, I will ask you if I need the details.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Please, Professor, we have no time to dwell on the details, on the actual facilities which were taken out. I am just asking you simply and honestly, as a person, as a human being, as an intellectual, obviously as you told us after several months, after five months you arrived in the city in which you had spent a good part of your life. Were you negatively impressioned? Were you appalled, simply speaking, by the extent of devastation that you saw then as a human being, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Relatively, yes. And later it got much worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You mentioned the passes which you actually called very vividly ausweiss. Do we agree that this happened sometime in June or July 1992? On the 8th of August -- of June, sorry, 1992. Do we agree that in that part of Bosnia and Herzegovina and in the immediate vicinity of Mostar there was still war?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please do not overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was it war or was it not war?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So it was war. So we agree that it was a time of war?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you agree would me that it would be only normal for the army to part -- that takes part in that war to set up checkpoints on roads to check the passage of civilians or of troops or of similar? Is that something which looks -- which you consider normal?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is normal for me for them to check my papers to establish my identity. I do not consider it normal to -- for you to be issuing an ausweiss. I had a normal identity card as did everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But these movement documents were also issued to Croats and other people living in Bosnia and Herzegovina, not just the Muslims. Everybody had to have one. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I did not ask any of the Croats whether or not they had to queue, but when I queued it was all the Bosnians that were queueing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You were born in 1947?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: 1945, I apologise. You were a military conscript, were you not? Under the law you were subject to the military obligation?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And to move around as a conscript, you would have to have because of your war duty station and schedule, you would have to have a pass for movement?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that was supposed to be issued to me by the army. They would have either had to release me or just make it possible for me to move around like a normal person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you will remember how the army boards maintained their records and whether it was in Mostar or Zagreb or wherever. Actually, military records were maintained by the civilian authorities, not the army. The civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there was no civilian authorities. The HVO had established HVO rule and a military dictatorship having eliminated all other bodies of authority in Mostar and Stolac and generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The document, the passes which you were issued were issued to you from the civilian authorities, civilian structures. Just tell me whether this is so or not. I don't know whether they were attached to the civilian authorities which were actually non-existent. I don't know how they regulated this because we could not have been issued documents from a non-existent civilian authority. I was just amazed at the fact that I had to be issued such as certificate, such a pass to be able to move around, whereas the front line was outside Mostar, outside the city, outside Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. At that time, the state, I mean the new, just emerged nascent state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which had a short time before that declared its independence from the rest of Yugoslavia, it was not functioning. Is that a fact? The central state authority was not functioning in every walk of life. Was it not? Was it?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was functioning. I disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: For the school year 1991 and 1992, or perhaps even better 1992, 1993, were the normal, regular decisions received from the ministry at your university regarding the budgeting, the financing, which are routine information that you receive every year from the ministry? You didn't get it that year; right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not that year, but we got it from Croatia that time, and it was interference on the part of another state in my state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So -- so you didn't get it from the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the decisions and the budget which you got normally every year before that?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So someone else encroached upon that territory trying to actually save instruction and the activity of the university?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, yes. I can say something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion in that area where you moved in limited scope to also come across checkpoints manned by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina also?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I didn't move in that direction. I took the only road which was possible and passable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But did you know that the troops distributed elsewhere had also other checkpoints manned by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never came across any such checkpoints. I never got in touch with any such people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Not even later talking to people? Even after the war were you acquainted with the fact that any such checkpoints existed?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you were not informed about any such checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You implied in a certain way that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna actually insisted on the Croatian language being used, and through these documents that we saw today, you showed the dissatisfaction of the intellectual echelons, especially in regard to language and so on and so forth. So you publicly voiced your opposition to the existing policy which was being pursued on that score in that period. Do we agree?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did anyone prevent your policies or, for instance, ban your gathering which we discussed a while ago?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one about the resolution, no. But they did prevent children from learning that language in school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But your activities were free?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were free to act. We were -- had some unpleasant moments but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm asking whether the authorities made your life difficult?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did, by sending some -- unorganised groups, disarrayed groups that actually shot -- opened fire around that building from automatic rifles and actually frightened us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: How do you know it was the authorities that sent those people to frighten you?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they were in uniform with the patch marks that indicated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But does this necessarily mean that they were sent bit authorities?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you don't know that for a fact?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no one to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you don't know that for a fact. It was your conclusion.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can someone just go around opening fire around a building and passing and circling in cars around a building and opening fire without the authorities having been implicated in any way? With actually harassing intellectuals who had a calm gathering to draw up a resolution? So I can conclude that it was the doing of the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Professor, you of course have the right to draw your own conclusions, but I want to ask you now that you have mentioned this. You agreed with me a while ago that it was war. You agreed that the state central authorities were not operative. So was it not under those circumstances peculiar that the troops or members of some army were just going around haphazardly shooting at random around the town? Does that make sense to you? Does it mean that someone told them, instructed them to do that? Look --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't happen the day before or the day after. It happened just then and just there, on that specific location. So one could conclude that it was not just a fortuitous incident. It was an organised thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The fact that the soldiers were opening fire into the air and that that happened, it just happened only in that particular day, never -- never in other periods?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only on that day in such an organised fashion. It was organised around the building of the faculty of the students' hostel. They circled around the buildings in their cars and opened fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And even though you think that that was engineered or directed, the authorities never sent you a representative or any document officially to tell you that you were not to do what you were doing?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We formed a council, a legitimate council of the Islamic Community which was also legitimate. So why would they forbid a legitimate organisation to draw up a document of this kind? There was no reason for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a few other words about this intellectual initiative or initiative of intellectuals. According to the documents that we have seen, I have not noticed in them a single person of Croatian nationality, but --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that was a resolution of the Bosnian Muslims in Herzegovina. But we protected everybody in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is quite clear what the resolution says. We have teen that. But your statement also implies also from some quotations from the documents that we saw that as intellectuals you were seeking to impose yourselves on the parties and on the situation that you were seeking changes. Why was this a monoethnic initiative? Do you think that the intellectuals on the --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All those who had something to bear on public life did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, that is your opinion?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is and I saw that and I talked to people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mentioned yourself that at the university there was a Croatian professor or there were Croatian professors that were not aligned according to ethnicity but according their own convictions?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Professor Bozo Coric actually left. I'm not condemning the Croatian intellectuals but the authorities that imposed themselves on this entire situation and overall life.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Despite the fact that the authorities were seeking to consolidate their ranks being in a situation of war, that didn't matter?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not trying to consolidate their ranks to make a multinational society, which is actually commensurate with multinational being.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You then also said that one couldn't enter Croatia except if one held an ausweiss, sorry.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Professor, does every sovereign state, every state, any sovereign state and the State of Croatia was certainly could have run at that moment, does it have the right to decide for itself what particular identification papers it will recognise in any legal transactions, legal operations? Do you consider that to be an entitlement of the state?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I consider that every state has a right, an obligation to take a stand in relations towards other states and not para-states, and these were para-states and para-statal documents. And that was the essence of the problem. Also, vis-a-vis the Republic of Croatia. We wanted them to make it possible for people to pass, to move about just like Croatian citizens could enter Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I just have another question, and then I will conclude my examination. Professor, of course your he expanding on this matter a bit. Is it the sovereign right of a state to recognise the documents issued by a rowers' society in Alaska -- a rowing society in Alaska, if it so wishes?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're not talking about -- yeah, but you're talking about the papers belonging to a rowing society, a rowing club, not a passport of a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, at that time an independent state, the government of which was completely isolated, the administrative services which were completely isolated, could it at all have been in a position to issue these papers? Did it, could it? It didn't issue them in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did. It did. People came with such documents from Sarajevo and Zenica and other cities, but they were return to Mostar so to be able to take out these documents in Mostar, Capljina, Siroki Brijeg, and only then return. Initially it was not a very -- attached very much importance, but later it became a rule. No one could pass with a document of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is also around Mostar and issue such a document. People exclusively had to have a different sort of identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Difficult to go back to the beginning. Do you agree that it is the sovereign right of any state to either recognise or not recognise the documents or any documents of somebody else? Yes or no? Please respond yes or no and then the Prosecution can ask you for additional clarifications. Is it the sovereign right of a state or not?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are not talking about border crossings and border control guards at the borders of the republic of Croatia. We are talking about people on this side of the border who were also returning people to get the proper documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. That concludes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kovacic. You have shown us document. Can you ask for that document to be tendered into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I thought that it would be tendered at the end of the cross-examination but I could do it now, no problem. Whatever is convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see the document. It was announced but I didn't actually see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Demirovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 3D 00182. So can I please have it admitted into the case file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is admitted under the reference 3D 00182.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, you said that you had another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have only one document. I have to put two or three questions to the witness and then I will tender the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to remind you that you have another 44 minutes for all those members of Defence counsel who will be taking the floor. The Defence has taken three hours so far. You have 3 hours and 44 minutes. As a result you have 44 more minutes. We will resume at about 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.35 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Coric, I give you the floor. I see you on your feet.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. Before the break you said that the two remaining Defence teams have 20 minutes each. Your Honours, the witness gave evidence yesterday for a bit more than four hours. He spent a lot of time speaking about me directly and the units that were under my command during war. You know very well that giving opinions about a certain period of time, especially if it is not truthful, requires a lot of time to disprove it, to prove that it was untruthful. I think that we will come across such situations many times during our trial with many other witnesses and testimonies. I'm not exaggerating when I'm saying that the witness didn't speak truth, but I ask that you give us additional time to establish the truth, and therefore, we need additional time. My Defence team needs additional time because we have 20 documents that we wish to tender into evidence that would help us establish the events and protagonists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Mr. Coric for your intervention. As everybody knows, we have been indicated that the Prosecution and Defence will have the same amount of time. In one of the Status Conferences held before the trial, I said that when it comes to individual responsibility of one of the accused, it would be appropriate to give the same amount of time to the Prosecution and the Defence. I also said that it would be good if Defence teams among themselves could decide on how to distribute the time among them. Now you have rightly pointed out that this witness during his testimony mentioned three names, the Accused Prlic, the Accused Coric, and the Accused Praljak [as interpreted].
