Thus, in this case it would be appropriate to split the time between these three accused primarily and to leave less time for other Defence teams. I'm also stating now that obviously the Defence teams did not manage to reach an agreement and thus we ruled that each team will have one-sixth of the time. As you know, there were some remarks made about lodging a appeal against this decision, and very soon we will rule on this issue. All of this means that if Defence teams are unable to reach an agreement among themselves the Judges will have to intervene. I said on a number of occasions that the counsel have to focus on significant essential issues and that they shouldn't lose time on less important issues. Unfortunately, sometimes we, the Judges, are just unable to understand the thrust of your questions. We tend to think that there is a good reason behind it and that you are aware of that reason, but nevertheless, we wonder what's the point of such questions. The fact is that the Prosecution initially said that they would require an hour and a half for a witness, and in reality this turned into four hours. Bearing in mind that the Prosecution used up exactly three hours and 44 minutes, that means that the same amount of time will be given to the Defence. Right now we have about 45 minutes of that time left. Before the hearing began, we, the Judges, wondered whether it would be a good idea to extend this time allotted to the Defence, but it all depends on the plans that the Prosecution have for completing the examination of three witnesses scheduled for this week. We should turn to Mr. Mundis now and see what he's going to tell us so that we can decide whether more time can be allocated to the Defence of Mr. Coric. Please go ahead, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I should also draw again to the Trial Chamber and the Defence that when we filed the chart indicating the linkages for these two witnesses this week that the revise the estimate for Mr. Rizvanbegovic was three hours rather than the initial 1.5 hours. Having said that, Mr. President, I anticipate that the next witness to testify, who I will not identify in open court, I expect that his direct examination will take no more than about one hour and 15 minutes rather than the two hours that he's down for. Consequently, I would expect that -- that we -- we perhaps could complete that witness's testimony today depending on the amount of time given to the cross-examination of this witness and the one that immediately follows. Now, the witness that -- the third witness for this week we would then expect would start tomorrow morning. We would have between tomorrow and Thursday approximately 10 hours of court time. I believe that the 65 ter estimate for the third witness this week is approximately four hours. Again, these are estimates as we've stressed repeatedly. These are estimates, and if we are able to commence that third witness first thing in the morning tomorrow morning, we do not believe there would be a problem completing his testimony by Thursday at 1400 hours or 14.15, the time that we're supposed to finish. But again, it depends on whether we can finish the second witness today or if there's a little bit of time for completion of that witness's testimony tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Do what you can. Mr. Coric would like to put all the questions that need to be put to this witness, so see what you can do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I realise that we are running out of time, and this is why I will not continue with my cross-examination of this witness, because I realise that there is no more time left. And I need something else to mention. You just said what accused were mentioned by this witness, and you mentioned General Praljak in that context. However, the witness has so far not mentioned him. I think that you misspoke, that it was a slip of tongue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't say Praljak. I said Pusic, Coric, and Prlic. The next counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Professor Rizvanbegovic, my name is Vesna Alaburic, and I'm a lawyer from Zagreb. I will be putting questions to you on behalf of General Milivoj Petkovic, one of the accused. You told us in April of 1992, Stolac was occupied by the Chetniks. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that at that point in time the local authorities in Stolac were composed of Zeljko Raguz, HDZ member, president of the municipality; Alija Rizvanbegovic, President of the Executive Board who at the same time was president of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Don't know, though, whether he was the president of the SDA. I know that he was a representative from that party, but I'm not sure about him being the president of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So when the Chetniks came to Stolac in April of 1993 [as interpreted], you said that Mr. Zeljko Raguz left Stolac. Mr. Rizvanbegovic remained in Stolac serving as the president of the Executive Board. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who at that time served as the president of the municipality of Stolac since Mr. Raguz had left?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the president of the Municipal Assembly served. I think he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Is that what you think?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The president of the Municipal Assembly. That's how these positions were split.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, during two and a half months of the Serb occupation, did the Muslim politicians cooperate with the Serbs when it came to municipal bodies?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They tried to convene the Assembly as much as possible in order to be able to function so that there would be some governing bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, was there any resistance to this Serb occupation on behalf of the Muslims remaining in Stolac?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean? What kind of resistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Any kind of resistance, armed resistance, silent resistance?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Silent, yes, but not armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, when the Croat forces liberated Mostar, was Mr. Alija Rizvanbegovic in danger of being arrested due to his cooperation with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I mean Stolac. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When asked by Ms. Nozica about the resolution of the Muslims of Herzegovina, you said that you organised it with support from the Muslim community because all other organisations collaborated with Herceg-Bosna. In order for us to understand each other and in order for the others to understand us, let us please clarify this term "collaboration," to collaborate. Would you agree with they that the term "collaboration "today in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, so in your state and my state, means cooperating with the enemy?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't say with the enemy. It's a bit too strong of a word. But definitely cooperation with those who have usurped the power.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So can we then conclude that this was a cooperation with somebody who was not your friend?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't say that. They weren't terribly friendly to me, if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that in view the dictionaries used in the former Yugoslavia, in them after the second world war the term collaboration meant cooperation with the enemy or the occupying forces and that it was used colloquially in that sense?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that it was so after the Second World War, but in this case when I use that word that's the type of cooperation that I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What kind of cooperation did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not recognise or respect the cultural identity of Bosniaks. They did not recognise the political aspect. They did not show respect for their state. They only showed respect for a parastate, and they collaborated with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, then, why did you say for Mr. Hadziosmanovic that he was a collaborator?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We, that's what I meant. He's the one.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In your view, was it desirable to reduce the number of so-called collaborators with Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have been happy not to participate in the protest that is we initiated.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the protests. I'm asking you in terms of your understanding of the word "collaborator." Was it desirable to reduce their number?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, and to have legitimate representatives.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In your view, would it have been desirable to remove from political and other offices the Muslims collaborating with Croats or Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were all removed from office, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that in the course of 1992 the number of Muslims who wanted to cooperate with the HVO or, rather, with Herceg-Bosna was reduced and that the number of Muslims who didn't want to cooperate with the Croats in Herceg-Bosna increased?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it had to do with the sentiment that prevailed at the time, that an apartheid was being created.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that such an attitude of Muslims to Herceg-Bosna had a direct consequence or effect on this situation in the units, military units?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us now go back to the resolution of the Muslims of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is the Prosecution Exhibit P 00974. Let us put item 5 to the witness, please, the second portion of it. 74. The resolution of the Muslims of Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not the one.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you check the number for me, please? I apologise it's the number 00374, 374. While waiting for that to appear, I'll refer to the second paragraph. In the second paragraph of item V, on the following page, it says: "We appeal to the defenders from the Muslim ethnic group to place themselves under the BH flag, and their sign should be the coat of arms with golden lilies." Who were the defenders who are being referred to here?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, the defenders were the ABiH and the HVO and the HOS, but we asked from the Muslims -- we asked that the Muslims bear insignia of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what sort of insignia are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The coat of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Which was?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lily.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So could this appeal refer to defenders who were already in the ABiH and fought under the sign of the lily?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They already had such signs.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So this can't refer to them?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it can.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But they were already -- they already had such signs. The only logical conclusion is that this refers to the Muslims in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It refers to all defenders. It's quite clear here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How can you request that they place themselves under such a flag if they're already under such a flag? How can you tell them to adopt a certain flag if that is already the case?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We wanted to say that all the Muslims who were in units defending Bosnia and Herzegovina should adopt the flag of Bosnia and Herzegovina, should fight under that flag. That means defend being the sovereignty and integrity of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that means that they -- those in the army and the HOS and the HVO should fight under that flag.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's clarify this message. The coat of arms of Bosnia and Herzegovina with the golden lilies, when was this law about such a coat of arms adopted?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but when Bosnia and Herzegovina was declared independent, that was the flag it had. That's what its coat of arms. It was on the 1st of March, 1992. That is when Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised as the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's when a referendum was held. But I don't know when this occurred exactly. It was during that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you remember which BH body adopted a decision according to which the coat of arms should be -- should consist of golden lilies?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a commission that worked on that before the war. I remember Professor Gavran who suggested that such a coat of arms should be adopted and I think that everything was prepared for this at the time, but as for when the decision was taken I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the date, I'm asking you about the body. Was it the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Was it the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When taking such a decision on the coat of arms were representatives of Serbs and Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina also consulted? Did they participate in that?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croats, yes, but I don't know whether Serbs participated in that. I think some Serbs also participated in the decision because there were Serbs in the Presidency and they remained for many years in the Presidency and in other bodies of power.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Does this answer also mean that you know that you know that the Presidency took such a decision?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know I. I know that the Presidency participated in this decision, that there were Serbs that were still part of the authorities. But as to whether they participated in this decision I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please slow down for the sake of the interpreters and could counsel please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they were still those who were elected.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me whether the golden lily is still what one can see in the coat of arms of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because a decision was adopted. There was a consensus, High Representative was imposed and then the flag was adopted. This was how it happened, but up until that point of time the coat of arms and the flag were the ones in the UN.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was the High Representative the one who should take such a decision because the Serbs and the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina were against the idea of golden lilies representing Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't personally answer that question. I think that the High Representative should have taken such a decision because the political parties couldn't agree. But as to whether these political parties were more Croatian or more Serbian I wouldn't really know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor Rizvanbegovic, with regard to this appeal to defenders to place themselves under the flag of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I would like to ask you something about the Muslims and the HVO. Are you aware of the fact that at the time in the Stolac area the percentage of Muslims in the HVO was significant? There were companies which were purely Muslim companies.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think any of them were purely Muslim ones. There were units in which there were more Muslims, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that shortly after this appeal and particularly at the beginning of 1993 we could see the first examples of Muslims leaving the HVO? And when leaving, they didn't return their equipment or weapons.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I'm not aware of the fact that it was possible for someone not to return equipment or weapons. This could only be done illegally, so it's difficult to believe. Perhaps there were separate cases but I'm sure it wasn't a mass phenomenon. I'm a civilian. I don't know about these things.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, at that time did you hear anything about Muslims or certain Muslims in the HVO having contact with the Muslim Bregava Brigade? Did you hear anything about them remaining in the HVO with an agreement? The agreement was to carry out certain actions against the HVO.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bregava Brigade wasn't called the Muslim Bregava Brigade. I think there were members of other ethnic groups. They weren't just Muslims. But I didn't hear of anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about the commander of the ABiH appealing to Muslims in the HVO to cross over to their own people?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about the position of the Croats in the area of Stolac in April 1993 according to which Mr. Alija Rizvanbegovic was still politically active, was in favour of entering Stolac with the military of expelling the Croats of establishing purely Muslim authority, and he was supported by the command of the Bregava Brigade in these efforts?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Alija Rizvanbegovic hasn't been politically active since April 1992. You're talking about April 1993 now so that has no meaning. At the time he was an ordinary civilian.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Professor, how can you say that he wasn't active politically at the time since up until the 12th of June he was holding office?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Up until -- from June.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Alija Rizvanbegovic, as President of the Executive Board, is he your relative?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's a relative of mine but he's not a very close relative. Was

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was he the owner of some building in Begova?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was it the second house?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the second one, marked with number 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I don't have a few more questions. I'll try to be brief. You said that on the 12th of June, 1992, Zeljko Raguz returned to Stolac. He was soon replaced by Andjelko Markovic.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that Andjelko Markovic was at the head of the HVO government that had been established. As to when that occurred, how that occurred, I really didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you say the HVO authorities, you're referring to the civilian municipal authorities?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were no civilian authorities. Military authority had been established.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What was Andjelko Markovic?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the president of the municipality for the military authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you distinguish between the HVO military authorities and the HVO civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume there were no civilian authorities. There was nothing called the HVO civilian authorities. I assume that there were some civilians who worked within those bodies, but officially there was no such thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have one more question. Can you please clarify something with regard to the Begovina complex? Were these the last buildings facing the Serbian positions or, rather, were they buildings at the very front line if you're looking from Stolac?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO line was to the north of Begovina. It was 200 metres to the north. The lines of the Serbian forces was several kilometres to the north from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But after Begova, apart from the hydroelectric power plant there were no lines?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no contact for several kilometres. Not a single shot was fired.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I didn't understand you. Could you please inform us as to the amount of time we have for the Defence in order to be able to organise ourselves?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Jonjic, how much time will you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you can see from the documents in front of you, I need quite a lot of time. When deciding how to answer my client's question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you mean when you say lot of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At least an hour, but bear in mind that during the break the Defence counsels discussed the matter, and for the next witness we'll have very few questions. So we could perhaps take some time -- some of the time that we have for the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll give you an hour. But before I give you the floor, I have a question I would like to put to the witness, which follows on from what was said a minute ago with regard to the flag that is now used in your country. With regard to the language, what is the official language right now? Is it Serbo-Croat, is it Croato-Serb, is it Croatian, is it Serbian, or is it the Bosniak language? Which is the official language used today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The official language, since the constitution for the Federation was adopted, is the Bosnian, Croatian, and Serbian language, and that's how they refer to the languages in all constitutional documents and other documents. So it's Bosnian, Croatian, and Serbian. And I'm saying this in alphabetical order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may. First you said Bosnian, Croatian, and Serbian language. Is it language or languages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Language. Whether they use the term language or languages in the constitution I'm not sure, but my answer refers to the name of the language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to the previous question, when one compares Serbian -- Serbo-Croat or Croato-Serb or Serbian and Croatian or Bosniak, are there any differences between these languages, differences that would allow one to say that such a such an individual speaks the Bosniak language, whereas some other individual speaks Serbo-Croat, and the third person speaks the Croatian language. Are you yourself capable of making such distinctions? As an example, I'll mention the French language. When a French person speaks a Canadian or Belgian person could understand person, but there are differences between the Belgian language, the Canadian French, and French. This is also the case in Switzerland, and similarly we have British English and American English. Nevertheless there are differences between the two languages. Differences may exist as far as you are concerned. Would you say that there are any significant differences that would allow one to categorise someone on the basis of the language that that person speaks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was the minister, I organised for the World Bank three experts, a Bosniak, a Serb, and a Croat, and they were from the faculty of philosophy in Sarajevo, and they were to draft a report which they did. They established that the language concerned was one language that was simply called Bosnian, Croatian, and Serbia, but essentially there was no difference between these various versions of the language. Perhaps certain differences have been emphasised or recently certain differences of vocabulary have been emphasised. For example, the word for bread. We can have a word such as "hleb" or "kruh" for bread, but such differences don't even amount to 2 per cent, and I'm talking about vocabulary now. As far as syntax is concerned there are no differences at the level of syntax. There are no phonetical differences either. So there are no significant differences. It's just a matter of different terms, and it's more of a matter of civil rights rather than a linguistic issue. I'm certain I haven't used a single word that someone present in the courtroom here has not understood. I've understood all the words used by everyone in the courtroom. There are no differences. Differences can be artificially emphasised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no significant differences, then why do you make it appear that this matter is a significant matter in relation to your programme for the Muslim intellectuals? Why -- why is this an issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, would you accept someone calling your language a different language, saying that Italian is not your language? The name of the language used is also an element of one's identity. So what was at issue was not the essence of the language, it was the name of the language. There are no reasons for an ethnic group not to use its own name for the language used. It was a matter of identity. There were no linguistic problems that had to be resolved. It wasn't a linguistic issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that clarification. And a very last question. A minute ago you said that when you were the minister you asked for a report to be drafted about this subject. Is this an interpretation error or were you a minister with a political function? Could you clarify this, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was the Minister of Education, Science, and Sport in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. President Izetbegovic -- and I wasn't the only intellectual who was a member of the government, but President Izetbegovic thought he should engage intellectuals who could participate the ministry's work. I accepted the post of minister, and I worked independently throughout that period of time, although I wasn't a member of a political party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can you tell me exactly when you were the minister?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From 1996 to the year 2000, to the end of the year 2000. I had two terms of office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unless I've made a mistake or this is the first time that we have heard about the fact that you were a minister from 1996 until the year 2000. Very well. It's now twenty to three. Mr. Jonjic, you ever one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon Mr. Rizvanbegovic. I'm Mr. Jonjic. I shall ask you quite a few questions on behalf of Mr. Coric. As actually this one hour would not suffice for all the questions I wish to put to you, I should just concentrate on the most significant issues, and if time should remain for something else, I shall also gladly ask you about these things. You being a professor yourself, you have questioned students in your time so that you know that students are wont to expand on their answers, so I would ask you to kindly refrain from doing that so we can use our time efficiently. Before we come to April, 1993, I should like to just ask you one question relating to your engagement in the Congress of the intellectuals of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Muslims intellectuals of Herzegovina, rather. You actually said that you were a member of the leadership of that Congress.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please would counsel and witness not overlap. I cannot interpret. I'm just unable to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: I didn't see that you actually distanced yourself from the positions advanced by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the interpreters. This is a consequence of our rush to say as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Namely, I failed to notice that you ever distanced yourself, disassociated yourself from any of the publicly voiced positions of that Congress, which means that in principle you agreed to everything that was said and published under the umbrella of the Congress of Bosniak Muslim intellectuals.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You referred to the Congress in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: All the Congresses from 1991, 1992 to this date?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Congress was actually appointed in 1993 in Sarajevo. I was not a participant then of its Assembly, but when I came to Sarajevo, they admitted me to the Council of the Congress.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: So subsequently, actually if I may say so, you espoused the programme documents and the tendencies of the Congress as such?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so much. It is only normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Today you said for the sake of the record, it's page 33, line 21 to 24, that precisely the Congress adopted a conclusion that Muslim people should then thenceforce be called Bosniak people and you said literally that this conclusion was binding on the legislative authorities?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not binding. It was the intellectual reaction to the situation of the -- of the people in terms of their name, given their long history in order to actually spare you vacuous students' stories.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Maybe there was a mistake in the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no mistake in interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: We can check it in the record.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said anything vacuous to my students.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: I would like to say that this Congress was held on the 22nd of December, 1992, that of Congress intellectuals in Sarajevo. A number of speeches were delivered there, one of them by Professor Dr. Mustafa Imamovic. Would you agree with me that he is one of the leading Bosniak intellectuals?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Professor Imamovic is one of the professors of the law school, one of the writers of the history of the Bosniaks, and one of the prestigious professors, intellectuals, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Would the registrar please show us document 5D 01062. While we are waiting for this document to be reproduced, the speech by Professor Imamovic, that is -- can I ask you, Mr. Rizvanbegovic, as we have no time to read the document through, the entire report, the entire speech, can we just take a look at a couple of highlighted sentences in it? As you can see here from the impression, Professor Dr. Mustafa Imamovic was in fact the president, the editor-in-chief, the president of the editorial board. Can we go on? Can we have the following pages, please? Can we go down a bit? Page 69 of the original. So here it's page 67. So it is actually the next image -- the next page, rather. So on the right-hand side, the lower underlined quotations which is actually the quintessence of the entire section. And Professor Imamovic says here "We can rightly say that everything that bears of the epithet Bosnian mainly refers to the Muslims here." The title of this article is the relationship of the Bosnian and the Muslim or the relation between the Bosnian and the Muslim. Would you agree with me, Dr. Rizvanbegovic, that this is a position which actually identifies Bosnia with the Muslims' causes concerned in the non-Muslim parts of the population or the non-Muslim peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this is not my attitude. Different intellectuals have different opinions on this, and this Bosnian Council is a council of peoples of different opinions, and thank God that that is so that we can communicate and exchange our different opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: But you didn't disassociate yourself from these positions.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But there is no reason for me to disassociate myself. I mean, we were discussing the matter. He was delivering his speech, transmitting his ideas. I had my views. There is no reason for me to disassociate. That was a discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Let us go to the basics immediately, I propose. So to April, April of that year. Yesterday, at page 32 of the record, you mentioned that when you were apprehended the members of the military police actually took you to the bone hospital. Is that the right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the 1st of July actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Do you know the names ever these people?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No he, I don't know the nails of these people. They didn't actually say who they were, they just put me in the car and took me away.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Were they from the Stolac municipality?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I don't know. I didn't know these young people either before the war or after the war. I was a professor who sat at home doing my work at home. I rarely went out to bars and such. I lived in Stolac and worked in Stolac so I didn't have an opportunity to meet many young people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: I apologise for the interpreters' sake. Page 70 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter believes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- of the record, of the transcript, when the Izetbegovic house was set on fire -- Rizvanbegovic house was set on fire there were guards standing guard in front of your house. They were Dragan Peric and Jozo Kresic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Do you know which unit to which they belonged? Were they soldiers at all?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were soldiers they were here on this line in Begovina. They were constantly in Begovina. My wife made them coffee and treated them to some cakes and so on, and they were there for days.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Will the registry please show us document 5D 01056. As you can see, Professor Rizvanbegovic, this is the military police in Stolac, and this is a wages bill from the 4th of June, 1993, for the military police. Is Dragan Peric and Jozo Kresic on this list?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a unit that was in Begovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: It is not?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And as far as I can see, none of these people were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Speaking about this list, having agreed that these --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were not military policemen. This was a regular HVO unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Can you see on this list of members of the military police of the HVO in Stolac on the 4th of June, 1993, identify anyone who could be a Bosniak Muslim?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Amir Medar is on this list. That's under number 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: And a bit lower down there, 29?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 29 Rasim Dedic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: And 31?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Semir Selimic. So it's three Bosniaks. Unless I've skipped over someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Would the registrar please go down, scroll this page down a bit more. So the last one you mentioned was Semir. And then after him we also have Edmin?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is Edmin, and there is a certain Marim.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: So there are at three Muslim members in Stolac on that particular take day; is that right. When Alija Rizvanbegovic's house was set on fire in Begovina. You said that then you went to see the different police. Do you know --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Do you know whom you talked to?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was an officer on duty, a lad on duty. I reported the case to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Did you actually lodge any criminal complaints against it?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I thought my reporting of the incident to them was enough for the police to do its work.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Am I interpreting regularly -- properly your words when I say that the Muslims in Stolac, that you say that the Muslims in Stolac were discriminated against as of the day Stolac was -- was liberated on the 1st of July, 1993, and even move after that?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Every day more -- more by the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Can we see document 5D 01052. The author of this document is -- you have already mentioned him, Professor. So we scroll down the page to the bottom of the page. The author is Ivica Kraljevic. The stamp is the administration of the military police. And can we go back to the top of the document, please. This is an official note from -- of the 21st of June, 1993, is it not, Mr. Professor [as interpreted], which actually notes that some violence had taken place? Will you help us identify what this is about?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an official memorandum. During the night between the 19th and 20th of June, 1993, between midnight and 2.00 in the morning, there were a series of explosions in the city of Capljina demolishing the next -- the following facilities owned by Muslims. The cafe Ribica, the cafe Saraj, the cafe Bel-Ami, the cafe Fike, the burek pastry shop owned by A. Kudro, the Izbor shop, the Sator-Komerc outlet, and the beauty parlour at Domanovici owned by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: So it is obvious we can conclude that the Muslims actually carried out on-site in this investigation and took further action.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a routine procedure. Nothing was actually done subsequent to such investigation. Perhaps you are able to see whether anyone was arrested following this demolition.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Will the registrar show us 5D 01053, the next document. The author of this document is the same. It is again Ivica Kraljevic. As you can see, Professor, this was drawn up on the 23rd of May, somewhat earlier, that is. And if you would be so kind as to assist us and read the second section -- second paragraph, rather, of this report, work report.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in the area of the municipality of Capljina? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I mean?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In the area of Capljina municipality, more specifically in the villages of Visici and Celjevo on the 16th 17 and 18 of May, there were three burglaries into houses owned by Muslims on which occasion all the foreign exchange and some technical equipment were seized. One of the owners was also beaten up. The persons were uniformed. The assumption is that they are members of the military police. On the 18th of May, we ambushed them and the persons were caught red handed. These are three former members of the HOS. And then also Bruno Busic. The persons are from Posusje and from Zupanja. They are in detention and investigative action is under way. The stolen goods have been found except the portion of the gold and the foreign exchange and they will be returned to the owners."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Will you continue?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During this period they were also detected and apprehended and detained three persons who had seized three cows which have been recommenced and there will be a criminal complaint lodged for that incident."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I apologise. I thought that the Prosecution had a reaction. Can the registrar show us yet another document from this period, which is 5D 01068. If you can, Professor, let us read together this entire report.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "During this period in the area of six municipalities the following activities unfolded. "During the mentioned period in Capljina there occurred a series of events against which were actually manifested as shooting in the city. Seven persons were apprehended. Their statements taken and he criminal proceedings shall be instituted against the same because of the jeopardy I to human lives. "In Stolac there was discovered a food store which was intended for the army of B and H, and according to an order of the government of the HVO Stolac, it was -- it was" -- can you scroll it up for the benefits of the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: But the interpreter still hasn't finished the first page because it is being read very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like to know what is the real advantages of all these documents to the witness in the situation of his particular house? I don't see any point in cross-examining this witness on this issue, particular issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What is the relevance?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that it is obvious that these documents show that what the witness claimed yesterday, namely that the Muslims were discriminated against, that their property was damaged and that nobody was punished for that is simply not true. These documents show what happened in the territory of Stolac municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All of this pertains to Capljina municipality. Nothing of this pertains to Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Rizvanbegovic, if you take a look, you will see that it says in the first sentence "In the territory of six municipalities." So that covers the territory including Stolac.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but everything that happened here happened in Visici, in Capljina, not in Stolac. Stolac is not mentioned except that a storage of food was discovered.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: All right. Would you now turn to the second passage?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's precisely what I was saying. This is the storage of food intended for the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: All right. Now skip the next paragraph and please read out the last one?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is evident in the atmosphere in Stolac is unfavourable when it comes to the attitude towards Muslims because it is evident that certain members of the Croat nation try at any cost to provoke them and to create incidents by verbally insulting them and threatening them, shooting at night, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Rizvanbegovic, based on the last paragraph, can we conclude that as was stated here, among the Croats there was not a single uniform attitude towards Muslims but, rather, that the head of the military police criticised MUP members for their unlawful conduct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this was done by members of MUP, what did the gangs do then?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about that. I'm asking you whether it can be concluded that based on this document the MUP had one opinion and the military police had another one.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the opinion of Ivica Kraljevic. He's the person recording and his police is responsible for doing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Would you please clarify this. What do you mean by "his police"?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police is reporting. Everybody is in uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Reporting, all right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now would the registrar please show us another document 5D 01055?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers please slow down for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 2nd of June, 1993. At the very bottom of the document I'm interested in the last paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the territory of Stolac municipality, MUP is creating significant problems or, rather, their members who try at any cost to create a conflict with Muslims threatening them that they would be moving them out to Bosnia, slitting their throats, that they are thirsty for their blood. They're also physically abusing them. There is a lot of shooting so that the population of Stolac is forced to seek protection from the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: All right. So now can we conclude that what happened there was not an exception but, rather -- but, rather, a systematic phenomenon? Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would, but I don't see that anything was being done about this. My impression was that nothing was done about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, after you were taken to the bone hospital or Kostana hospital, you said that you were interrogated.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I asked to be interrogated because they said they would take me for an interview, and I thought that I would be interviewed and then they locked up in the basement. And I asked to be interviewed to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: And they hit you there?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Do you know who hit you there?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some military police. I don't know who he was. I asked in the corridor where was Mr. Puljic. I think that that was the name of the commander. I said I wanted to talk to him and then he hit me and then I fell back down into the basement. And that was all. I had no further contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, at the time when you were taken to the bone hospital were there any patients there?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: No? I apologise to the interpreters once again. Would the registry please show us document 5D 01057. While we're waiting, Professor, I'd like to ask you this: Do you know where patients from the bone hospital were?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the patients were taken to Blagaj. Now, as to the time, I don't know that. I was under house arrest, so I don't know that. When I came there, I didn't see any patients I only saw the military police. As for what happened afterwards, I can't say, because I was in the house from April on and then afterwards I had no opportunity to see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: We have the original in Croatian. This is dated 10th of June, that is to say just a little bit before you arrived. This is a document of the 1st brigade of the HVO signed by commander Obradovic where he says something about the cleaning and the accommodation of -- for the bone hospital patients who were in Capljina. Under item 3, you will see that they were in the premises of the medical corps of the brigade in Capljina. So is it true then that they were not transported to Blagaj but, rather, to Capljina?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood this document correctly, this has to do with the cleaning ladies. It seems that -- well, the hospital in Stolac had over 100 patients. Not just two persons, more than 100 persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Would you please read out item 3?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The said persons worked while the patients of the bone hospital were in the premises of the medical corps of the brigade in Capljina."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: So it has nothing to do with cleaning ladies but the patients.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it has to do with two patients.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers please not overlap and slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please scroll down? I can't see the top of the document. In view of the current situation with the patient in singular, patient in singular of the bone hospital who is located in the medical corps of the barracks an inability to use the prisoners in order to clean the premises where they're accommodated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: What about this, "where they're accommodated"? Is that plural or singular?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me see this. It says here "In view of the current situation relating to the patient of the bone hospital who is located in the medical corps of the barracks an inability to use the prisoners in order to clean the premises where they're located." Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Who is accommodated?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We see that this relates to just one single patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Could the registry please scroll down the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour. Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I have an objection. The witness appeared in the hospital, was taken to hospital on July, on the 1st of July, 1993. This is a document relevant to the 10th of June, 1993. What is the relevance? What is the point in cross-examining on this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What is your aim here, Mr. Jonjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the purpose of this is to show that the claim of the witness is not true, namely that the patients were transported to Blagaj. The other purpose is to show who was in charge of the bone hospital. If I may continue, I would like Professor to tell me this:

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Does item 1 refer to patients in plural, and does item 3 refer to patients in plural, or is it singular?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here, "To provide two cleaning ladies who used to work in the bone hospital," obviously they don't work there any more, "to clean the premises where the patients of the bone hospital in Capljina are housed."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Is it plural?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's plural, but what does it prove? Item 3: "The said persons," meaning the cleaning ladies, "would be working while the patients of the bone hospital were in the brigade in Capljina."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are overlapping. The interpreters are unable to follow this exchange.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see what this is about. We're going in circles and wasting time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry. Every second sentence our interpreters are completely out of breath. You must observe two things. First, you must speak slowly. Second, you must not start speaking before the other speaking has clearly -- the other speaker has clearly finished. You are overlapping. You are starting to answer before the question is finished and the next question perhaps comes before the answer is finished. This is impossible. You will not reach your goal, namely that we understand this conversation. If we cannot follow it, it is completely lost time. Please, I implore you to have some discipline in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. You are right, and I apologise for everything that I should be blamed for. All of this is a result of the lack of time and the abundance of documents that I would like to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise as well, but I'm tired. I've been sitting here the entire day under very difficult circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: I'd like to start from the date, 1st of July, 1993. And I'd like to see document 5D 01064. I think that that's the one I need. I apologise, 065. Professor, let us keep the numbers and would you read the text, please.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Order in relation to the authorities of CP in towns. In view of the newly created situation and in order to censure safety of citizens and cities and their property, I hereby order. "1. Security of the town and citizens of Capljina and Stolac and that of their property shall now be taken over by the civilian police of Capljina and Stolac, which will have full authority in order to prevent looting and violence. "2. In order to implement this order, I shall hold responsible commanders of civilian police of Capljina and Stolac."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Would the registry please scroll down the document all the way down.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is forwarded to the commander of civilian police of Capljina, commander of civilian police of Stolac, archives, signed by the commander of Sector South, Colonel Nedjelko Obradovic. And if we go back up we will see the date is the 3rd of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Can we go back up, please? We see this is the 3rd of July, 1993, which is 15 to 20 days before the Begovina complex was burned down. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Can we conclude based on this that the responsibility for the safety of citizens and property, including in Stolac, was in the hands of civilian police?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we cannot conclude that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because in Begovina there was army. The civilians had no access to Begovina. All access to Begovina was secured. My wife was unable to enter her own house because the army was there. There were guards. There were guards. There were people in positions on the lines. So there was no possibility to access that area in view of the terrain and the roads leading to it. Nobody could reach that area without the army knowing about that. They were in the house of my brother and controlled the entire area. There's a huge yard, a courtyard that is the size of 20 courtrooms, and nobody could enter that area without the army knowing about it. And nobody else had access. Civilian police had no access there. They could only come there with the authorisation of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Was this signed by a commander?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Could we see document 5D 01064, please.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we are waiting, can I ask something? Why didn't he order his unit to look after the houses that they were housed in, especially since this was the monument classified as the first category monument?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: We don't need to go into that right now. Could we please see the document 5D -- oh, yes, we can see it here. Once again, this is a document -- if you allow me, Professor, I will go through it.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, so that we don't waste time with reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Once again this is the document of the 1st Brigade of the HVO, the same date, 3rd of July. In the preamble we can see that the person who signed the document observed that there were frequent violations of law and order. And then under item 1 it says: "Any cases of stealing or disappropriation of property is to be prevented and the perpetrators are to be punished and proceedings instigated against them through this command." Therefore, not only the measures are prescribed here but also the procedure that was to be applied. If we scroll down, we will see that under item 4 once again it is ordered that based on the UN Charter and Geneva Conventions, the civilian population be protected in the area of responsibility of the brigade. And then at the very bottom we can see that this document once again is signed by -- can we see page 2, please? Once again, it is signed by Mr. Nedjelko Obradovic, commander of the 1st Brigade. We can see that this was forwarded to all units of the 1st Brigade, to the Ljubuski company, to the head of the SIS or security and information service, and then ONO, I think, stands for the operations and teaching body.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may say, if I were in Nedjelko Obradovic's shoes, I would resign immediately because it was obvious that nobody was following his order. So what kind of a colonel was he?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we come to the moment when you were transferred from the bone hospital to Dretelj. Did you know the people who transported you there?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These people were very young. I didn't know these people. There was a driver and another escort who was armed. You said that they used the Nazi or Roman salute or the Hitlergruss, as was said.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned Mr. Mehmed Dizdar and his book on Stolac yesterday.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He wrote a book. It was his personal vision.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I started -- I grew angry when I started reading it because I don't agree with many things he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: But to -- in that book he mentioned the facts that you mentioned today, namely that the HOS in Stolac was to a large extent composed of Muslims. There wasn't a HOS unit in Stolac. It just entered the town but carried on, moved on. But because of what was happening with their attempt to expel the Chetniks, to make sure that they didn't stop at lines that had been agreed on, they went to see Kraljevic, because he said that they would move on, they would go further on. That's why there was this massive phenomena?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: They went into the HOS?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Is this part of the tradition of the Independent State of Croatia? Does HOS have to do with that?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. All I saw is they had black uniforms on them. They had the slogan "Ready for the homeland," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: So the Muslims who were in HOS also used the same salute?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You don't have to go into it. When those people realised what was at stake they left the HOS. So there were no longer any Muslims in the HOS and they were in a terrible situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Very much. Let's into the go into that. Mehmed Dizdar left the HOS on that day. I think that's mentioned in the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Here we are again. Please calm down. Slow down. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Professor Rizvanbegovic, yesterday you mentioned something that seemed contradictory to me. First you said that the security of Dretelj was provided by the military police. That's where you were detain. And then later on page 38, line 15 to 18, you said that you did not know what sort of insignia the guards guarding you had because -- or the soldiers guarding you had because it wasn't important for you at the time. How would you explain that then?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the barracks themselves, I don't know about the surroundings because I couldn't see the surroundings themselves. Kreso Rajic was one of them. I knew him and he had military police insignia on him. I asked who was providing security for us. He said it was the military police. And Palameta said this too and I know it was the military police providing security for these premises and you can see that Ivica Kraljevic is a member of the military police from the documents. As to who provided security in the surroundings, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the registry now show us the following document 5D 01059. Professor, if you have a look at the date the date is the 2nd of July. That is the date that you arrived there or the day after you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: It's an order for providing security for the Dretelj prison. Item 1 "Immediately establish a homeland unit the strength of which should be 40 men for the purposes of guarding the prison and barracks in Dretelj." And then the procedure followed is described. Could we scroll down.? Could the registry scroll the document down right to the end of the document so that the Professor can tell us who signed the document. Unfortunately we can't see the signature in this electronic version but if we have a look at the English translation the signature might be legible, might be visible when the document was scanned as part of the document was missed out but you can see that it's a document from the brigade. You can see the English translation here. Professor, could you say who signed the document?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that 40 homeland members wouldn't have been sufficient to provide security for that camp. I assume there were men around the camp, but in the camp itself there were only young people. There were no elderly people. At least I didn't see them through the window.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Do you assume this or do you know this?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the people who were outside were not members of the homeland units, of the Home Guard Units. They were young men. Those would beat others -- I'm talking about those who would beat others and those who would come up to the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Why are you referring to elderly people now? I do apologise, because I don't recall using the adjective elderly so far.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, while I was free members of the Home Guard Units were elderly men, whereas men at the unit, et cetera, were younger people. They were under 35. Members of the Home Guard were over 35. They were sort of reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: After you were arrested do you know how men were recruited and how they were organised?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't know about that in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Of course. So you don't know this either. Thank you very much. On page 42, yesterday you said that medical care in Dretelj was poor. It had only been organised after a while, after a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Could the registry please show us the following document 5D 01061. I think we have it on the screen now; is that correct? This is a document signed by Kresimir Bogdanovic, the commander of the 3rd Company, the 3rd Battalion of the military police in Capljina. The document was issued on the 2nd of July, a day after you arrived there, is that correct? Or on the same day?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The day following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: And the document states that in the Dretelj barracks there are many detained individuals, some of them who complain about their health condition and are requesting medical care. "Therefore, we request a medical team be sent as soon as possible." As you can see, this was sent to the Bozan Simovic barracks. Do you know where that is?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: If the registrar scrolls down a little to the end to the bottom of the document we could have a look at those it was forwarded to.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the medical clinic Bozan Simovic, the 1st HVO Brigade Knez Domagoj and the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps these doctors visited the place, but that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Could we have the following document 5D 01066. This is a document from the 1st HVO Brigade dated the 5th of July, three days after this request. It's an order on establishing a medical commission to provide detainees in Gabela, Dretelj, and Heliodrom with medical care. It's signed by -- can you tell us who it's signed by, Professor? It's signed by --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nedjelko Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: And it's been forwarded to the 1st and the 3rd Brigade of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The commission was formed after five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, do I have another five minutes? Another ten minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rizvanbegovic, yesterday you mentioned a security member in Dretelj hitting you.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Do you know the name of that person?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know the name. At the very outset I said I didn't know very many names I didn't know those young people and in particular over there, there weren't many people whom I could have known.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Have I remembered this correctly? The person who hit you, he forced you to stare at the sun?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: How long did you have to stare at the sun?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until I went blind.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: You can't say how long that was?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Have you suffered permanent consequences or has your sight suffered permanent consequences?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you can tell I constantly have tears in my eyes and I can't stare at snow. It's very difficult for me when the sun is very strong, et cetera, so, yes, I have suffered certain consequences. So when I went to Zagreb, I immediately reported to Durnja Falisavac, a colleague of mine. She took me to the clinic. Her sister works there, and they took certain steps to deal with this problem. So, yes, I haven't gone blind but I do suffer certain consequences. At the time, however, I was in a very bad state.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Could you identify some of the members of security force who acted in a more brutal or cruel way?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one of most brutal ones was Palameta. He was one such person. I know him from Stolac I didn't know the others. I don't know who they were. These people were young people, members of the police, people who had come from the front lines and created problems, beat people up, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: In a couple of sentences could you describe the terms you were on with Ivica Kraljevic who signed a number of documents we have already seen today?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war or during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Both?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war we knew each other that was the case for the all the other citizens we would greet each other and that's all. And I've describe the sort of meetings I had with him when we met, when I was in Dretelj, in the prison in Ljubuski as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Did Kraljevic treating brutally did he apply force?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: In a couple of sentences could you describe your relationship with Mr. Tomo Sakota?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Tomo Sakota quite late. I was very surprised when we started discussing the matter that he was the commander of the camp in July I thought when he arrived there things had changed obvious that wasn't the case this only happened later I met him when I got onto that lorry and when he got me off the lorry. And he favoured me. He would let me go now the into the grounds, walk around. There was a prisoner repairing a car. He would let me walk up to that prisoner. I could do this once or twice, at most. Whenever he appeared he would greet me and that was something for me, that meant something to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Why were you treated in a particular way? Why did Sakota, as you yourself have said, drive you from Ljubuski to Capljina.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that some of my friends contacted him and asked him to do this. I think that's the reason and as you can see he was in favour of human rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Yesterday when you mentioned Esad Suta you also mentioned my client Valentin Coric?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Coric ever go to Dretelj, did you ever hear about that?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw him and the first say we moved around I think Mr. Suta said there weren't be any problems since there were three of us. We weren't aware that there would be a camp there we thought we would interviewed again and he would ask Valentin to do something for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Did he hear that Mr. Coric was in Dretelj? Did anyone else tell you that?
