utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Did anyone tell that you Mr. Coric released someone from Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only mentioned Mr. Coric within the context I mentioned earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to Mr. Anicic or Andjic [as interpreted] who you call the Dretelj commander?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we saw the document you were released on the 23rd of September; is that correct, 1993 I apologise you were not released you were transferred to Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: And in the document we saw yesterday, we could see that there were certain security measures had been ordered when you were released or, rather, transferred. You interpreted this by saying that they said you to be particularly dangerous?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because I was handcuffed. There were no windows on the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could the Court usher help us and place the following document on the ELMO. Unfortunately we do not yet have the electronic version of this document.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that document yesterday for the first time, the one that was signed by Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: We'll now see the document dated the 23rd of September. The Chamber and Prosecution have both the Croatian original and the English translation. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: You can see that it's the same date, the 23rd of September?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: And that's when you were transferred to Ljubuski under the security measures mentioned. Can you please read through the document or perhaps I should do it. It might be better. On the 23rd of September, 1993, 541 detainees were supposed to leave Dretelj. They were supposed to be transferred in eight buses. You didn't mention through the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm trying to be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: At about 1700 hours at the gates of the barracks women and children refugees from Bosnia started to gather there and they protested against the release of the detainees and they insulted the military police. At 1800 hours large group gathered and they started pushing vehicles onto the road of the car park before the barracks to block the exit. When Mr. Rade Lovric, the deputy of the military police, arrived we received an order to create a live shield and a quantity let so that we could provide a safe exit for the vehicles from the convoy. Half an hour later from the barracks Bojan Simovic a lorry full of sand was brought in with the intention of blocking road. The military police intervened. The lorry was removed and Argo Pavlovic, the driver, was taken in and handed over to the criminal service for processing. He said that he had done this as ordered by the psychologist in the Knez Domagoj and the psychologist's name was Sandra Jovanovic. Ivan Anic [phoen] signed the document, the commander of the 5th military police. Professor Rizvanbegovic, can you see from that document that when you were transferred to Ljubuski under particular security measures, women and children, refugees from Bosnia, attacked the military police in an attempt to obstruct the release of detainees?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This obviously took place after I'd been taken out. This was a significant time after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Do you think it was difficult to anticipate that refugees from Bosnia would react in this way?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this action on the part of the refugees had been organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: That's your opinion?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is something I've witnessed on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: How could you have witnessed such a scenario if you were already in Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not on that occasion, but these are things that happen often elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Very well. When you arrived in the military investigation prison in Ljubuski, did you receive any post?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did get one in Ljubuski via the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Did you get any passes?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Do you know the name of any guards in Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know -- I knew a chap named Milos. He had brought me a message from my sister about this problem with Professor Franges. Actually, the action which was taken by Professor Franges. I don't know his surname. His name was Milos.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: And you do not remember anybody else?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Except for Ivica Kraljevic of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Suta there with you?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Did you try perhaps to address Valentin Coric through him?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I didn't know Mr. Coric, and there was no reason for me to reach -- to try to reach him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Through Suta you tried nothing?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I don't see why he should have treated me differently from the other people because we didn't know each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Tell me, please as this seems to be our very last minute, and perhaps I will not be able to show any other documents, yesterday presenting to us the documents about your exit in December, 1993, the -- in regard of the name of Perica Jukic you concluded that this was the SIS security and information service head. That is at page 9 from line 21 to 23 of the transcript. Why did you think that Mr. Jukic was the head of the SIS?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time they didn't mean anything to me. I only met him later. Because I thought the police had to give such an authorisation, an approval. That was a generally known thing. It was common knowledge that unless SIS granted such approval. One couldn't do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: But a minute ago you were talking about the police and not the SIS.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I hope that SIS is a part of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would have more questions, but I obviously have to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you will have to finish because you have just exhausted your hour. All right. Yes, Mr. Coric, you can have the floor under these -- these conditions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should like to thank you for the time allotted to me, but I should like to say that if we continue to have a debate conducted in this way, we cannot talk about a fair and regular trial. This -- this trial will become a farce. And I do apologise for having to say to this. Apart from the time allotted to us, we have some key matters which we have to discuss and which have remained undiscussed, and I can only imagine what awaits us in the future. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Jonjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I should like these 10 or 12 documents that we have presented to the witness to be admitted into the file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall do that right now. Will you please indicate which documents you wish to be tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are 5D documents. Their numbers are 01052, 01053, 01055, 01056, 01057, 01059, 01061, 01062, 01064, 01065, 01066, and 01068. And in addition to that there is a document that we only showed on the ELMO and which I hope will either tonight or tomorrow morning be part of the electronic system, and that document is 5D 01079. So can we have that document also, please, tendered into evidence. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Will the registrar tell us how these documents shall be admitted into the file.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... admitted under the following references: 5D 01052, 5D 01053, 5D 01055, 5D 01056, 5D 01057, 5D 01059, 5D 01061, 5D 01062, 5D 01064, 5D 01065, 5D 01066, 5D 01068. While we are at it, I take the liberty also to clarify that the following two exhibits tendered earlier this day are admitted under the following references: 2D 00007 and 2D 00017. The last thing regarding exhibits: For the record, the following two exhibits, 2D 00019 and 2D 00023, are respectively the very same exhibit as those admitted by the Prosecution today as P 00374 and P 09579. Thank you very much for these matters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just to avoid any misunderstanding, this sole document that we didn't manage to have in the electronic system, can we just have it recorded and the registrar didn't mention it. It's 5D 01079. Just that one document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Registrar. Is this exhibit admitted?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 079. I repeat for the record. 5D 01079. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Professor, your testimony has just ended, and you have given evidence for over eight hours, answering questions of both sides. On behalf of the Judges of this Trial Chamber, I thank you for having come to The Hague. I wish you a happy journey home and a fruitful continuation of your activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we shall adjourn our session for 20 minutes, and we shall continue at 16.05.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall resume our session. Before we usher in the witness and with the safeguards requested, I believe that the Prosecution has forgotten two documents. Mr. Mundis, which two documents are we referring to that have been forgotten?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Just for the sake of record, Exhibit 3842 and Exhibit 4667 were referred to during the examination-in-chief and were tendered by the Prosecutor, but for some reason they were not on the transcript. I would like again to tender these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I invite the registrar to admit these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, can you quickly say why this witness requires protective measures? We shall of course then work in closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Witness BI, can you tell us briefly about conditions of life in Stolac in 1992, beginning in the early part of 1992?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1992, to be more precise in March or April, the Bosnian Serbs withdrew from Stolac. HVO units entered, and together with the Bosniak side they represented some sort of a defence for the town. Life carried on almost as usual. Instead of going to work, people would go to the front lines. Some people were nervous of the civilian defence responsible for repairing houses that had been damaged as a result of the Serbian -- the Serbian shelling of Stolac. The situation was normal when there was no shelling.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Apologies, Mr. President and Your Honours. It has come to my attention that the accused cannot hear the testimony of this witness. There may be some problem with the sound system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we check the equipment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A technician will be arriving. Mr. Registrar, where is the technician coming from, from the centre of the town or from the neighbouring office? Mr. Praljak is raising his hand, so everything must be okay now. Mr. Mundis, please proceed. If there are any problems, inform us immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Witness BI, at the time the technical problem arose you were telling us about Serbian shelling of Stolac. Can you recall the approximate time period when this Serbian shelling of Stolac occurred?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs were in Stolac for three or four months in 1991 and at the beginning of 1992. At the beginning of 1992 they withdrew from Stolac, and that's whether the shelling started.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Witness, on page 142, line 16, you told us "HVO units entered." Do you recall approximately when it was that HVO units entered Stolac?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Can you describe the situation in Stolac after April 1992, that is, after the HVO entered the town of Stolac?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the town seemed quite damaged as a result of the Serbian shelling. Instead of going to work, the men went to the front lines. They were defending the town, in fact. The situation was normal apart from the fact that there was shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Witness BI, what type of damage Stolac sustained as a result of the Serbian shelling?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the damage was minor was the result of the shelling. Some of the roofs of the houses in town had been damaged. That's what the damage amounted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Witness BI, at this point in time, that is approximately April 1992, can you tell the Trial Chamber what the ethnic composition of the population of Stolac was?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were Bosniaks and Croats there. They represented the majority of the inhabitants, and perhaps there were seven or eight families of Serbian ethnicity that remained in Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Witness BI, can you tell the Trial Chamber approximately or the approximate location where your family lived in April 1992, in the town of Stolac?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Witness BI, can you tell the Chamber how your father was employed in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, he was employed by the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in what capacity?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an ordinary labourer. He -- he'd clean the streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Witness BI, can you tell the Trial Chamber what the reaction in Stolac was at the time the HVO arrived after the Serbian withdrawal?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reaction was a normal one. They were treated as liberators of some kind. There was quite a lot of joy as a result of their arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because when they arrived, the Serbs withdrew from Stolac. That meant that it was easier to move around and that people were not so afraid any more. They were a form or a sort of protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Witness BI, how long did the HVO remain a form or sort of protection in Stolac?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that was the case up until May 1993. I don't know the exact date. I don't know when the relationship between the Bosniaks and the Croats actually started deteriorating.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Witness BI, can you tell us a little bit about the conditions in Stolac between April 1992 and May 1993? What was life like in the town of Stolac in that period, that 13-month period?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the one hand life was quite normal. People lived from humanitarian on the whole. The factories were not operational. Anyone who was fit for military service would receive a salary from the HVO, if he was a member of one of their units, and that's how things were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Witness BI, what were you doing between this period April 1992 and May 1993?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a boy at the time, and I was mostly interested in -- in boys' games.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: What times of boys' came back place in Stolac in April 1992 through May 1993?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there weren't that many children of my age in town. When there was no shelling, when the day was calm, I'd usually play football.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: How about school? Did you go to school during that period?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mainly because the school wasn't open because of the fear of shelling. And then secondly, there were not enough pupils. There weren't any teachers as some had left with the Serbs. Others had fled to Croatia. There were very few people in Stolac at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a few moments ago as reflected on lines 9 and 10 of page 145 that the relationship between the Bosniaks and the Croats started deteriorating. Can you describe for us a little bit about how that deterioration occurred?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The relationship started deteriorating when they started arresting intellectuals. That's what happened in the beginning. And then they started arresting ordinary citizens, too, citizens between the age of 16 and 17 and up to the age of 60 or 70. They arrested anyone who represented a potential threat or to the HVO soldiers. They arrested anyone who was fit for military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: When did these arrests take place? When did they start taking place?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From May up until the 3rd of August, 1993. While I was in Stolac, people would be arrested every day. Initially, they arrested people on a massive scale, and subsequently they arrested those who were hiding.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Witness BI, if you know of the ethnicity of the people who were being arrested in this period from May until 3 August, 1993, in Stolac.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Witness BI, did you ever personally observe any people being arrested in Stolac between May and the 3rd of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw quite a lot of people being arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Can you describe for us a little bit in general terms about what you saw?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw HVO soldiers taking away some of the male inhabitants. They had their hands in the air. They would usually gather them in two or three places in Stolac, and when they had sufficient number of them they would drive them away to Dretelj, Gabela, and the Heliodrom, to Ljubuski. This is what I subsequently found out.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Let's me ask you, sir, a couple of follow-on questions. You told us they would take away the male inhabitants. What about the females?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Women and children lived in great fear, because those HVO soldiers -- well, most of them were drunk every day. They would open fire. They would insult people. So there was a lot of fear. The people who remained in Stolac were very afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Witness BI, you told us just a moment ago, page 147, lines 9 and 10, "They would usually gather them in two or three places in Stolac." Can you tell us, Witness, what locations you were referring to, these two or three places in Stolac?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when they first started arresting people, this would be in the centre of the town behind the department shop where they would round up between 20 to 30 individuals. They would then take them away. Then there was the Kostana hospital, the steelworks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about the Kostana hospital? What was that?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be a little clearer? Before the war or during the war? Could you rephrase your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Before the war, what type of hospital was the Kostana hospital, if you know?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can remember, it was the hospital where bone fractures were treated, where rheumatism was treated and other bone diseases, where is as during the war it was the main hospital in Stolac, and that is where the wounded and others were taken to. It was the only hospital that functioned during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Witness BI, can you tell the Trial Chamber what happened to your family during this time period between April 1992 and May 1993?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My family remained in Stolac, but we didn't live in our own house. We moved to the lower part of town where most of the inhabitants were, and we lived with a relative of ours or, rather, we lived in his flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Witness BI, why did your family move to a different location in Stolac.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Primarily because the part of Stolac I lived in was frequently exposed to Serbian shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: And, Witness BI, can you tell the Trial Chamber what happened to your family after these arrests began in June and July of 1993?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I was living in my own flat. My father had been taken away to a camp. I don't know the exact date. I know that it was in July. My mother, brother, and I stayed on there for another 15 to 20 days, and then we were driven away to Blagaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness BI, let me ask you about this time when your father was taken away to a camp as you told us. Do you recall any of the specific details about that day? And, if so, can you please share those memories with the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, I can't remember any specific details. On that day I wasn't at home. I was at the playground or at the stadium. But according to what I was told later on, two HVO soldiers appeared. He was in his slippers and shorts as it was summer. He was standing in front of the door. And they sort of asked him to go with them, and they said that he didn't have to take anything with him. They said he would be returned immediately, that they only wanted to conduct an interview with him, but he did not return.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you say he did not return, do you mean permanently or do you mean for a certain period of time?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't return for a certain period of time to Stolac. Later, he returned to Blagaj after seven or eight months.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Did your father tell you where he was during that seven or eight-month period when you didn't see him?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. In Dretelj and in Gabela.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Can you describe your father's appearance when you first saw him after this period of time when he had been in Dretelj and Gabela?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he looked older than he was. He looked about 15 years older than he was. He used to weigh 90 kilos, but when I saw him he only weighed 60. It was quite simply impossible to recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Can you describe, Witness BI, for the Trial Chamber the situation in Stolac from the time your father was arrested until you and your mother and brother were, as you put it, driven away to Blagaj? Can you describe that period of time?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a difficult period of time. We lived in great fear. There were -- there was something on fire every single day. There was shooting every single day. Soldiers came and maltreated and insulted the people. Terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness BI, when you say there was something on fire every single day, can you tell us a little bit about what you mean by something on fire every single day? What did you see on fire?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, houses burned every day. The museum. Private houses as a rule, mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about the events in Stolac in the middle of July, 1993, when you saw some buildings on fire?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was a participant in one of these fires, but when I say participant, I was on the other side because I helped extinguish a fire, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- first of all, do you recall the approximate day, month, and year that this incident took place where you participated in extinguishing a fire? Do you recall the approximate time period of that?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot recall the exact period. Perhaps it was sometime between the 15th and 25th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Witness BI, can you please tell the Trial Chamber what you remember about that day. What happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day I was at the playground of the elementary school which is not far away from my house. I was there with several of my peers, peers of Croatian ethnicity, and we were playing football. In the afternoon I went home for lunch. It may have been 3.00 or 4.00 p.m. As I passed across the old Tepa, I saw smoke billowing from the courtyard of the mosque. And boys will be boys; we were curious. We were interested to see what was happening. So I went into the mosque yard, and from the yard into the mosque itself, and I saw that at the very gate a carpet had been set on fire. So I pulled that carpet out, and at that moment or perhaps within the next three or four minutes while I was trying to put out the fire, the carpet which was on fire, the entire compound of the mosque went up in flames, and the flames billowed high, sky high.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Let me brief interrupt you there, Witness BI. You say on line 8 at page 151, "I passed across the old Tepa." Can you tell the Chamber, please, what the old Tepa was?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a Tepa or the Tepa is a flea market. It is a market first of all, generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: And Witness BI when you talk about going into the yard of the mosque, do you remember the name of the mosque that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm referring to the mosque which is in the centre of Stolac, which is Sultan Selim's mosque which is better known under the name of "the Tsar's" or "Emperor's" mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness BI, I interrupted you at the point where you were talking about -- you said the mosque went up in flames, the flames billowed high, sky high. Can you tell us what you saw next?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that moment, the mosque was not on fire and there were not flames that were sky high. It was the surrounding buildings that were on fire at that particular moment when I pulled the carpet out of the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: And where did you go next? What did you see after you pulled this carpet out?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went back up there some 50 metres from that place, and I watched on as those houses were burning. And within some 10 or 15 minutes, the mosque was set on fire again. And in the second Tepa, I'm sure they used some gasoline or some stuff that you use for arson. So indeed the flame could soon be seen billowing through the roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness BI, how long were you at this location watching these buildings on fire?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there for about 10 or 20 minutes. Then soldiers came who had been outside the school in Stolac, and this school is not far from the place of the fire, perhaps some 50 or 60 metres. So these soldiers came and drove us away. I continued to watch the fire, however, from the window of my house, which is not far away.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Witness BI, who were these soldiers? From what military were these soldiers from?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: HVO, for at that time only the Croatian Defence Council existed in Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: And when you say, Witness BI, that you continued to watch the fire from the window of your house, where exactly was your house in relation to the Sultan Selim mosque?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was about - sorry - about a hundred metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Witness BI, did you see any efforts by anyone to extinguish these fires that were burning on this day?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask with the assistance of the usher that the witness be shown a number of photographs and a map. What I'm going to propose that we do is place or identify these locations of these photographs on this map and then we'll tender all of these materials as one in-court exhibit. I would ask first that the witness be shown the photograph -- yeah, that's the right photograph. This has been previously been marked as P 09583. But again, with your leave, Your Honours, we would propose that all of these materials go in as one in-court exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: First of all, Witness, do you see the photograph that's on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Can you please describe what you see in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the centre of Stolac, the mosque, the elementary school, and a part of town, a settlement called Cuprija.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness be given the thin red marker.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Now Witness, if -- we're going to mark on the photograph that's to your right. Not on the computer screen but on the photograph to your right. If you look to -- yeah, that one. You told us, sir, that you saw the elementary school. Can you please put an S for skola on the school building?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Can you please put a -- well, where do you see the mosque in the picture? Do you see the mosque in the future?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Can you please put an M on the mosque.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness BI, you told us earlier about the old Tepa. Is the old Tepa visible on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a part of it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Can you please point to the part of the old Tepa that is visible on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can just discern the roofs under the pines here, and the entire compound around the mosque. Of course, it should be taken into account that the buildings to the left also belong to the old Tepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: All right. Witness BI, I'm going to ask you if you could please with the marker -- you've told us about the entire compound around the Dzamija, around the mosque. Can you please circle the compound around the mosque that you've referred to as the old Tepa.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness BI. Now, I take it from what you've told us that your house where you were living is not visible on this photograph; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. It is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Can you simply at the edge of the photograph mark an arrow pointing in the direction to which your house was located?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Witness, I would ask if you could just put the initials BI in the lower right-hand corner of this photograph and today's date, which is 23/5/2006.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd ask now the witness be shown the map or the chart, the sketch, which was previously P 8986. This is page 7 of what was P 8986. If this could be rotated, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Witness, have you seen this -- have you seen this map sketch before?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is the first time I see it. Actually, I saw it for the first time when I arrived in Holland.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: One of my colleagues showed you this sketch, did they not?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Witness, since that time have you had an opportunity to familiarise yourself with this sketch?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us, Witness BI, what this sketch is a drawing of?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a layout of downtown Stolac, the centre of Stolac, including a part of other settlements, but, mind you, this is a very old sketch. But the section that we need is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: I think if the AV booth can zoom out just a little bit. That's fine. Thank you. Now, Witness BI, do you see on this sketch -- do you see the elementary school or the primary school that you marked on the previous photograph?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: And again, sir, if you could please put an S on that part of the map where the school is located.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please -- if you see it, can you please mark the mosque with the letter M.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Witness BI, now can you please, just as you did on the photograph, can you please draw a line around the old Tepa, that is the entire compound known as the old Tepa.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, I'm going to ask if it's possible to place the next photograph, which is the exact one the usher -- ma'am, if you could just put them both on there, actually, if that's possible. If we can zoom out. This was the photograph that was previously marked as P 09582. And if that could be -- that one. Yes, please. If that could be placed above the map if that's possible so that they're both visible on the ELMO. No. Place the map so that we can see them both. Maybe one on top of the other. And if we could then zoom out. Okay. Witness, let's take the photograph, then, and put it so that you can see it full screen. Thank you. Sir, can you please in the bottom right-hand corner of that photograph just put the number 1. Put the number 1, please.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Witness, what is depicted in this photograph? What is this? What are these buildings?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These -- these buildings are a part of the Tepa. They are to the right of the minaret. Actually, their wall is -- the back of their wall is in the courtyard of the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: And, Witness BI, can you tell us approximately if you have an idea when this photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I actually walked through Stolac already at age 5 or 6, and I really can't tell. Maybe in the 1970s or -- but they're older, older than I am in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Witness. Let's try a different question. Was this photograph taken before the war or after the war?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can see, first of all, that the shops are opened. The lorry which was sort of a truck service, towing service, was there. You can see the auto -- automobile association sign there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Now -- yes.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And you can see that the windowpanes are entire, that they have not been shattered by the detonations, by the blasts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: And, Witness, if I went to this location today, would it look just like this?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could say that what looked like that 70 per cent, because some 70 per cent of it has been renovated, because 70 per cent is in private hands, but the exterior and also the interior would be somewhat different.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could go back to the map, please. And, Witness, if you could please mark what we just saw, that photograph that you marked as number 1, can you mark that area on this sketch?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I note the time, Mr. President. I'm afraid unless you want me to continue, we're going to have to stop for the evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As we've been sitting since 9.00, it's time to adjourn. Witness, you've taken the solemn declaration, which means tonight you will be dining alone. You should not discuss matters with another witness. You shouldn't speak to any other witnesses, and you should likewise not meet any members of the Prosecution or of the Defence teams. So you will be spending this night alone. You should be back here tomorrow for the hearing that will start at 9.00. The Victims and Witnesses Unit will take care of you. And if everything goes as planned, you should be able to go back to your country at the end of tomorrow. We haven't planned for you to stay on for one additional day. So as a witness, you understand that you should not meet anyone. I wish everyone a good evening, and I will see you here tomorrow morning at the hearing that will start at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 24th day of May, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.34 p.m.,
